options.text: Prescribe ibuprofen 10 mg/kg orally three times daily for 5 days, gentle range of motion physiotherapy and outpatient orthopaedic review in 2 weeks if symptoms persist
options.rationale: Ambulatory NSAID therapy misses the diagnosis and permits ongoing weight bearing that can progress a stable slip to unstable, dramatically increasing avascular necrosis risk.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.text: Order urgent AP and frog-lateral pelvic X-rays, immediate strict non-weight bearing on crutches and refer urgently to the on-call orthopaedic team for probable in situ pinning
options.rationale: The obligatory external rotation on hip flexion in an overweight adolescent is classical for a slipped upper femoral epiphysis, which is a surgical emergency; strict non-weight bearing is essential to prevent further slip and avascular necrosis.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.text: Order an MRI of the knee and both hips within 48 hours with orthopaedic outpatient review to plan definitive management after imaging is available
options.rationale: MRI is not the initial modality for suspected SUFE; plain AP and frog-lateral pelvic X-rays are diagnostic and available urgently, and any delay in immobilisation risks progression.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.text: Arrange bone scan and refer to endocrinology for hypothyroidism and growth hormone screening as a metabolic underlying cause before orthopaedic intervention is planned
options.rationale: Endocrine workup for SUFE is done later in atypical cases (very young, very underweight); the immediate priority is imaging, non-weight bearing and orthopaedic pinning to prevent further slip.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol 500 mg orally four times daily, reassurance about likely Osgood-Schlatter disease and a physiotherapy referral for quadriceps strengthening review
options.rationale: Osgood-Schlatter presents with tibial tubercle pain, not hip external rotation deformity; misattributing SUFE risks catastrophic progression and femoral head necrosis.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

explanation.summary: Referred knee pain in an overweight adolescent with obligatory external rotation on hip flexion is classical for a slipped upper femoral epiphysis. Diagnosis is confirmed on AP and frog-lateral pelvic X-rays. Management is immediate strict non-weight bearing and urgent orthopaedic referral for in situ percutaneous screw fixation. Delay risks further slip and avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
key_points: Adolescent hip or referred knee pain with external rotation = suspect SUFE
AP and frog-lateral pelvic X-rays are first-line imaging
Immediate strict non-weight bearing until definitive fixation
Definitive treatment is in situ percutaneous screw pinning
explanation.pearls: The contralateral hip develops SUFE in up to 40 percent of cases; unilateral SUFE under age 10 or over age 16 warrants endocrine workup for hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency or renal osteodystrophy.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

stem: A 9-month-old previously well boy presents to your emergency department with his mother, who reports 6 hours of episodes where he suddenly starts crying, draws both legs up to his chest, then settles quietly for 15 to 20 minutes before crying out again. He has vomited twice, most recently a small amount that looked greenish. His last nappy 30 minutes ago contained slimy red jelly-like material. He is now floppy between the episodes and hard to wake for feeds.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 40, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 37.4 C, cap refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Between episodes: pale, hypotonic, drowsy but rousable; abdomen soft with a firm sausage-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant; empty right iliac fossa; nappy contents as described
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.32, lactate 3.2 mmol/L (<2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.text: Abdominal X-ray series (supine and erect) to identify a target sign, dilated loops or free air before proceeding to more advanced imaging or surgical consultation
options.rationale: Plain films are neither sensitive nor specific for intussusception; a normal X-ray does not exclude it and they delay definitive imaging.

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast to identify a lead point and any associated bowel ischaemia before contacting the surgical team
options.rationale: CT delivers significant radiation to an infant and delays reduction; ultrasound is the AU first-line and CT is not required in typical presentations.

options.text: Trial of intramuscular ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg with 4 hours of clinical observation and repeat clinical examination before ordering any radiological investigations
options.rationale: The classical triad of colicky pain, redcurrant stool and a palpable mass is a surgical emergency; observation with antiemetics wastes the window before ischaemic bowel develops.

options.text: Urgent abdominal ultrasound performed by an experienced operator to look for a target sign and to guide the paediatric surgical team's decision on air enema reduction
options.rationale: Ultrasound has close to 100 percent sensitivity for ileocolic intussusception in experienced hands and is the AU first-line diagnostic step, allowing air enema reduction to be planned rapidly in stable children.

options.text: Take directly to theatre for laparotomy and manual reduction on clinical grounds without waiting for imaging as the classical clinical triad alone is diagnostic and time is critical here
options.rationale: Direct-to-theatre bypasses non-operative air enema reduction, which is successful in 80 to 90 percent of stable ileocolic cases and avoids anaesthesia and surgery in most.

explanation.summary: Intermittent colicky pain with knee-drawing episodes, a palpable sausage-shaped mass and redcurrant jelly stool in an infant aged 6 to 24 months is intussusception until proven otherwise. Abdominal ultrasound is the AU first-line diagnostic modality with a target or doughnut sign. In stable children, air enema reduction succeeds in 80 to 90 percent of ileocolic cases. Signs of peritonitis, perforation, or shock mandate operative reduction.
key_points: Colic + redcurrant stool + sausage-shaped mass = intussusception
Ultrasound is first-line imaging in AU
Air enema reduction succeeds in most stable cases
Operative reduction if peritonitis, perforation or shock
explanation.pearls: Recurrence after air enema reduction occurs in about 10 percent, usually within 48 hours; children are typically observed for a minimum 24 hours after successful non-operative reduction before oral trial and discharge.

stem: A term 5-week-old formula-fed infant is brought to your GP clinic by her mother because she still looks yellow. Birth weight was 3.4 kg and she now weighs 4.6 kg with normal weight gain. Her mother reports that her nappies contain pale-white stools and her wee looks dark like apple juice over the past week. She is otherwise feeding well, alert and interactive between feeds. She was born vaginally without complication and has no family history of liver disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Jaundice extending below the umbilicus; sclera icteric; abdomen soft with liver edge palpable 3 cm below costal margin, firm; spleen not palpable; no dysmorphism
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 165 micromol/L, conjugated bilirubin 62 micromol/L (<20 micromol/L or <20 percent of total), ALT 145 U/L (<40), GGT 340 U/L (<50); FBC and film normal, blood group compatible, TFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent same-day referral to the paediatric hepatology unit for confirmation of biliary atresia by HIDA scan and liver biopsy with a view to Kasai portoenterostomy
options.rationale: Conjugated bilirubin above 20 percent of total or above 20 micromol/L in a jaundiced infant beyond 2 weeks is biliary atresia until proven otherwise; Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days of life dramatically improves outcomes.

options.text: Reassure the mother that this is likely breast milk jaundice or delayed physiological jaundice and review in 4 weeks with a repeat serum bilirubin at that visit
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated; conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is always pathological and demands urgent workup, and the infant is formula fed.

options.text: Commence phototherapy at home and repeat serum bilirubin in 48 hours to check the trend before deciding on further evaluation or hospital-based investigations for the persistent jaundice
options.rationale: Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and is contraindicated in conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia where it may cause bronze-baby syndrome; the priority is diagnostic referral, not phototherapy.

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid 20 mg/kg/day orally and arrange outpatient hepatology review in 4 to 6 weeks with repeat liver function testing before that appointment
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid may be adjunctive but does not treat biliary atresia; delaying referral by 4 to 6 weeks pushes the Kasai window and native liver survival falls sharply after 60 days.

options.text: Order TORCH serology and metabolic screening (urine reducing substances, plasma amino acids, galactose-1-phosphate) and review results before deciding on any referral pathway
options.rationale: Metabolic and TORCH screens are part of the workup but must not delay hepatology referral for biliary atresia; the Kasai window is the driver of urgency here.

explanation.summary: Any jaundice beyond 2 weeks of age (3 weeks if breastfed) requires a split bilirubin. Conjugated bilirubin above 20 percent of total or above 20 micromol/L is always pathological and biliary atresia is the do-not-miss diagnosis. Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days of life offers the best chance of native liver survival, so referral is same-day to a paediatric hepatology unit. Pale stools and dark urine strongly support obstructive cholestasis.
key_points: Prolonged jaundice past 2 weeks needs a split bilirubin
Conjugated fraction above 20 percent or 20 micromol/L is pathological
Pale stools + dark urine = obstructive cholestasis pattern
Kasai before 60 days maximises native liver survival
explanation.pearls: Time to Kasai is the strongest modifiable prognostic factor: 10-year native liver survival is around 50 percent when performed before 60 days but drops to under 20 percent when performed after 90 days.

stem: A term 3.6 kg male newborn on your postnatal ward has not passed meconium 52 hours after birth. He has started vomiting greenish material with the last two feeds. His abdomen is distended and tympanic. Rectal examination causes a gush of gas and loose meconium. He was born vaginally at 39+5 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy. His mother had gestational diabetes controlled on diet and there is no family history of cystic fibrosis or gastrointestinal disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 52, SpO2 97 percent, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Marked abdominal distension, tympanic to percussion; audible bowel sounds; per rectum: normal anus, high tone; gush of gas and loose meconium after examination; no anal pit or fistula
data_table.Investigations: Antenatal screening normal; newborn screen taken day 2, results pending; abdominal X-ray shows dilated bowel loops with paucity of gas in the rectum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Sweat chloride testing on day of life 14 to exclude cystic fibrosis after ensuring adequate weight gain and hydration prior to arranging the definitive test
options.rationale: Sweat testing is used for meconium ileus workup but is age dependent and does not explain the classical explosive gush; Hirschsprung is more likely and time critical.

options.text: Trial of a warm normal saline enema 10 mL/kg with observation for spontaneous passage of meconium then reassess feeding tolerance over the next 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Empirical enema may temporarily decompress but risks delaying diagnosis of Hirschsprung and does not address the underlying aganglionic segment that mandates surgical planning.

options.text: Contrast enema with water-soluble contrast to identify a transition zone and refer to the paediatric surgical team for suction rectal biopsy to confirm Hirschsprung disease
options.rationale: The delayed meconium, bilious vomiting, distension and explosive gush on rectal examination are classical for Hirschsprung disease; contrast enema shows a transition zone and rectal suction biopsy is the AU diagnostic standard.

options.text: Upper gastrointestinal contrast series to evaluate for malrotation and volvulus given the bilious vomiting before considering lower gastrointestinal contrast studies or rectal biopsies
options.rationale: Malrotation is important to consider with bilious vomiting but the transition-zone pattern on abdominal X-ray and rectal exam findings point to lower obstruction; lower contrast study is the correct next step.

options.text: Anorectal manometry to test the rectosphincteric inhibitory reflex within 24 hours before proceeding to any imaging or surgical review as this is more specific for aganglionosis
options.rationale: Anorectal manometry has poor accuracy in the neonatal period due to immaturity and is not the initial diagnostic step in AU; contrast enema and rectal biopsy are standard.

explanation.summary: Failure to pass meconium beyond 48 hours with bilious vomiting, abdominal distension and an explosive gush on rectal examination is the classical presentation of Hirschsprung disease. Contrast enema identifies a transition zone from narrow aganglionic distal bowel to dilated proximal ganglionic bowel. Rectal suction biopsy confirms absence of ganglion cells and hypertrophic nerve trunks. Definitive management is a pull-through procedure once the infant is stable.
key_points: Delayed meconium past 48 hours plus bilious vomiting warrants urgent workup
Explosive gush on rectal exam is highly suggestive of Hirschsprung
Contrast enema identifies transition zone
Suction rectal biopsy is diagnostic gold standard in AU
explanation.pearls: Enterocolitis is the major early complication of untreated Hirschsprung, with fever, distension and bloody diarrhoea; it carries mortality up to 20 percent even after surgical correction and mandates aggressive resuscitation with rectal washouts, IV antibiotics and surgical review.

stem: A previously well 12-day-old term male infant is brought to your regional emergency department floppy and grey after 2 days of poor feeding and vomiting. Birth weight was 3.5 kg; today he is 3.0 kg. He has been passing normal urine. Newborn screening samples were taken on day 3 and results are not yet back. On examination he is peripherally cool with prolonged capillary refill at 4 seconds and looks profoundly unwell. He has hyperpigmentation of the scrotum and penile shaft is prominent for age. There is no family history of endocrine disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 190, RR 62, SpO2 96 percent, temp 36.4 C, cap refill 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: Ashen and mottled; sunken fontanelle; dry mucous membranes; hyperpigmented scrotum; virilised external genitalia; abdomen soft with liver edge 2 cm below costal margin; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Na 118 mmol/L (135 to 145), K 7.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), glucose 2.1 mmol/L (2.6 to 5.5), urea 12 mmol/L (2.5 to 7.0), creatinine 96 micromol/L (<40), VBG pH 7.19, HCO3 12 mmol/L (22 to 26), lactate 4.5 mmol/L (<2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV bolus 20 mL/kg Hartmann solution over 15 minutes and empirical IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg to cover late-onset sepsis while awaiting blood culture and lumbar puncture results
options.rationale: Hartmann contains potassium and worsens the hyperkalaemia in a salt-losing CAH crisis, and sepsis workup alone misses the definitive adrenal replacement that is life-saving.

options.text: IV dextrose 10 percent bolus 2 mL/kg to correct hypoglycaemia and IV furosemide 1 mg/kg to force diuresis for the hyperkalaemia while further electrolyte studies are sent to laboratory
options.rationale: Furosemide worsens hypovolaemia in a shocked infant and does not treat the mineralocorticoid deficiency; hydrocortisone plus volume plus calcium is the correct initial bundle.

options.text: IV bolus 20 mL/kg normal saline over 15 minutes and IV dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg stat as it provides pure glucocorticoid activity without confounding future stimulation test results
options.rationale: Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and hydrocortisone at stress doses covers both requirements; the future stimulation test can still be performed after hydrocortisone if needed.

options.text: IV bolus 10 mL/kg 5 percent human albumin over 30 minutes and start IV insulin actrapid 0.1 unit/kg/hour with continuous cardiac monitoring for the hyperkalaemia
options.rationale: Insulin risks profound iatrogenic hypoglycaemia in an already hypoglycaemic infant; the priority is hydrocortisone, saline resuscitation, dextrose and calcium for cardiac protection.

options.text: IV bolus 20 mL/kg normal saline with 5 percent dextrose over 15 minutes, IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat, IV calcium gluconate 0.5 mL/kg 10 percent for cardioprotection and urgent NETS retrieval
options.rationale: This is a salt-losing CAH crisis: hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and shock in a virilised infant; parenteral hydrocortisone plus fluid, glucose and calcium for hyperkalaemia is immediately life-saving before any biochemical confirmation.

explanation.summary: A vomiting, dehydrated male infant in the second week of life with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia has salt-losing congenital adrenal hyperplasia until proven otherwise. Virilisation of the external genitalia and hyperpigmentation support the diagnosis. Immediate management is IV hydrocortisone plus normal saline with dextrose plus calcium gluconate for cardiac protection against hyperkalaemia. Hartmann solution and insulin are contraindicated respectively due to potassium content and hypoglycaemia risk.
key_points: Sodium low, potassium high, glucose low in week 2 infant equals CAH crisis
Hydrocortisone stress dose is definitive treatment
Normal saline with dextrose - not Hartmann - for resuscitation
Calcium gluconate cardioprotection when K above 7 mmol/L
explanation.pearls: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for approximately 95 percent of CAH and salt-losing crisis typically presents in the second week when maternal cortisol has waned; save serum for 17-hydroxyprogesterone and renin before giving hydrocortisone if the sample can be taken without any delay to treatment.

subtopic_detail: Cyanotic newborn - TGA vs pulmonary atresia
stem: A 6-hour-old term newborn on your rural nursery has central cyanosis noted on first feed. He was born vaginally after uncomplicated pregnancy weighing 3.5 kg. He has no respiratory distress and feeds well when calm. Antenatal ultrasound was performed at 20 weeks locally and did not identify a cardiac abnormality. A hyperoxia test with FiO2 1.0 for 10 minutes shows pre-ductal SpO2 rising only from 76 percent to 82 percent. Chest X-ray shows a narrow mediastinum with an egg-on-side cardiac silhouette. Femoral pulses are equal and easily palpable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148, RR 46, SpO2 76 percent room air pre-ductal, SpO2 82 percent post-hyperoxia, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Central cyanosis, mild tachypnoea, no recessions; single loud second heart sound; no murmur; femoral pulses equal; liver at costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray: narrow superior mediastinum, egg-on-side cardiac silhouette, oligaemic lung fields; hyperoxia test as above; VBG pH 7.32, lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2)

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.text: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn; commence inhaled nitric oxide 20 ppm, intubate for high-frequency ventilation and start dopamine 5 microgram/kg/min inotropic support
options.rationale: PPHN in this classical XRay pattern is very unusual and inhaled NO alone will not improve TGA saturations without mixing; failure to give PGE1 would allow ductal closure and death.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.text: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return; commence PGE1 infusion at 10 nanogram/kg/min IV, intubate and refer for urgent surgical repair as PGE1 alone will not stabilise this lesion sufficiently
options.rationale: Obstructed TAPVR shows a small heart with pulmonary oedema, not an egg-on-side silhouette; and PGE1 may worsen obstructed TAPVR by opening the duct further, so is contraindicated.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.text: Tetralogy of Fallot with hypercyanotic spell; give morphine 0.1 mg/kg IM, knee-to-chest positioning, IV fluid bolus and beta-blockade to increase systemic vascular resistance and improve saturations
options.rationale: Tetralogy typically presents later with a systolic murmur and boot-shaped heart, not egg-on-side; and hypercyanotic spells occur beyond the first weeks, not the first hours.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.text: Transposition of the great arteries; commence PGE1 infusion at 10 nanogram/kg/min IV, intubate for retrieval and arrange urgent NETS transfer to a cardiac centre for balloon atrial septostomy
options.rationale: The egg-on-side silhouette, narrow mediastinum, minimal hyperoxia response and single S2 in a well-perfused cyanotic newborn are classical TGA; PGE1 maintains ductal mixing and balloon atrial septostomy is the definitive rescue.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.text: Critical aortic coarctation; commence PGE1 infusion at 10 nanogram/kg/min IV, intubate for retrieval and arrange urgent NETS transfer for surgical repair via subclavian flap or end-to-end anastomosis
options.rationale: Coarctation would show absent or delayed femoral pulses and preductal-postductal SpO2 differential, not egg-on-side; hyperoxia response is usually better and cyanosis is not the dominant presentation.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

explanation.summary: A cyanotic newborn with a failed hyperoxia test (post-oxygen pre-ductal SpO2 remains under 85 percent), narrow mediastinum, egg-on-side cardiac silhouette and single S2 has transposition of the great arteries until proven otherwise. Immediate management is PGE1 infusion to maintain ductal mixing, intubation for retrieval and urgent transfer for balloon atrial septostomy. Definitive repair is the arterial switch operation in the first 2 weeks of life.
key_points: Failed hyperoxia (post-O2 SpO2 <85%) plus egg-on-side XR equals TGA
PGE1 maintains ductal mixing and is life-saving
Balloon atrial septostomy improves mixing before arterial switch
Definitive: arterial switch in first 2 weeks of life
explanation.pearls: PGE1 is contraindicated in obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous return because opening the duct increases pulmonary blood flow into an obstructed drainage pathway; that lesion is the one cyanotic newborn where PGE1 causes harm and it requires immediate surgical repair.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

stem: You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 3-year-old boy after five days of unremitting fever to 39.6 degrees Celsius. His mother reports he has been miserable, not eating, and his eyes have become red without any discharge. On examination you find a diffuse maculopapular rash across the trunk, an erythematous strawberry tongue with cracked lips, and a single tender left cervical lymph node measuring 1.8 cm. His hands and feet are firm and swollen with a dusky red hue over the palms and soles. There is no pus behind the tonsils. His BCG scar is inflamed. Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 30, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: white cells 18.2 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), platelets 542 x10^9/L (150-400), CRP 148 mg/L (<5), ESR 78 mm/h (<15), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), ALT 78 U/L (<40)
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent bulbar conjunctival injection with limbic sparing, brawny oedema of dorsum of hands and feet, injected pharynx without exudate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg single infusion plus anti-inflammatory-dose aspirin now
options.rationale: The child meets classic Kawasaki disease criteria: fever five days or more plus at least four of five principal features (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oropharyngeal changes with strawberry tongue and cracked lips, extremity changes with firm swelling, polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy >1.5 cm). Sterile pyuria, hypoalbuminaemia, thrombocytosis after day 7 and the inflamed BCG scar support the diagnosis. Australian and RCH guidance is IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary aneurysm risk from ~25% to ~4%, plus aspirin at anti-inflammatory doses (30-50 mg/kg/day) until afebrile for 48-72 hours then low-dose antiplatelet. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin plus paired blood cultures for suspected scalded skin syndrome
options.rationale: SSSS causes generalised superficial desquamation with a positive Nikolsky sign and painful skin, not conjunctivitis with strawberry tongue and extremity oedema. Blood cultures would not be first-line here and flucloxacillin does not address the vasculitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin 33 mg/kg every 8 hours for scarlet fever and general practice review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Scarlet fever from group A streptococcus can share the strawberry tongue and rash but presents with painful pharyngitis, exudative tonsils, and a sandpaper rash rather than five days of fever with bilateral conjunctivitis and extremity oedema. Kawasaki disease requires urgent IVIG within the 10-day treatment window. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Give a single dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone plus oral amoxicillin for likely bacterial cervical adenitis
options.rationale: Isolated cervical adenitis does not explain the multi-system findings and rash. Antibiotic monotherapy for a suspected bacterial neck infection would miss the diagnosis and delay coronary-protective IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Reassure the family this is a viral exanthem and discharge with oral fluid and paracetamol advice
options.rationale: Five days of fever with bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral changes, extremity oedema, polymorphous rash and cervical adenopathy fulfil Kawasaki criteria and mandate hospital treatment. Missing the window increases coronary aneurysm risk substantially. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: This child fulfils fever plus four of five classic Kawasaki criteria on day five, with laboratory features (thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria, transaminitis) that raise the pre-test probability further. IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days of fever onset is the coronary-protective intervention. High-dose aspirin is added for anti-inflammatory effect. A baseline echocardiogram is performed on admission.
key_points: Fever 5+ days plus 4/5 principal criteria diagnoses Kawasaki (incomplete Kawasaki uses labs)
IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion within 10 days reduces aneurysm risk from ~25% to ~4%
High-dose aspirin 30-50 mg/kg/day until afebrile then 3-5 mg/kg antiplatelet dose
Baseline echocardiogram on diagnosis; repeat at 2 and 6 weeks
explanation.pearls: IVIG dose 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours as one infusion; if fever persists 36 hours after infusion, repeat IVIG plus consider methylprednisolone or infliximab.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 4-month-old infant with a 2-day history of coryza and worsening cough. He was born at term and is otherwise well. Feeding has dropped to 40% of usual over the last 12 hours. Wet nappies remain regular. On admission at 22:00 you commenced nasal prong oxygen at 1 litre per minute for SpO2 of 87% and moderate work of breathing. It is now 00:15. The nurse reports his SpO2 has settled at 90%, respiratory rate has come down from 68 to 56, and he took 60 mL of formula 45 minutes ago without vomiting. Chest examination reveals widespread wheeze and fine crackles bilaterally with mild subcostal recession.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, respiratory rate 56, SpO2 90% on nasal prong 1 L/min, temperature 37.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Work of breathing: Mild subcostal recession, no head bob, no grunt, alert and consolable
data_table.Feeding: 60 mL of 90 mL feed taken 45 minutes ago, no vomiting, 3 wet nappies in last 12 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Escalate to high-flow nasal cannula humidified oxygen at 2 L/kg/min inspired flow now
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance reserves HFNC for infants who fail to improve on low-flow oxygen after 1 to 2 hours, defined as persistent hypoxia despite low-flow, worsening work of breathing, or increasing respiratory rate. This infant is stable on low-flow with SpO2 within the acceptable target range and improving respiratory rate, so premature escalation adds no benefit while consuming a scarce resource. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Continue nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and reassess response 1 hour after commencing oxygen
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance targets SpO2 90% or above, uses nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min as first-line oxygen, and formally reassesses at 1 to 2 hours. This infant has met target saturation, respiratory rate is trending down, work of breathing is mild, and enteral feeding is tolerated. Continuing the current plan and reassessing is the correct action. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with reassessment of work of breathing 20 minutes later
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended for bronchiolitis under 12 months. AAP and RCH advise against routine salbutamol, which does not improve length of stay, oxygen requirement, or admission rate in bronchiolitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Switch to nasogastric feeds at 100 mL/kg/day and cease all oral feeding for 24 hours
options.rationale: NGT feeding is indicated for bronchiolitis when work of breathing is moderate to severe, respiratory rate exceeds 60 sustained on oxygen, oral intake drops below 50% of maintenance, or the infant cannot coordinate suck and breath. This infant just took a full feed volume and has improving work of breathing. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Wean nasal prong oxygen off completely and check room-air saturations 10 minutes later
options.rationale: The infant is only 2.5 hours into oxygen therapy and remains on 1 L/min to hold SpO2 at 90%. Trials off oxygen are typically considered after sustained SpO2 above 92% on minimal supplemental oxygen with settled work of breathing, usually the following morning. Weaning now is premature. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: RCH bronchiolitis pathway uses low-flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min as first-line oxygen with SpO2 target of 90% or above. Escalation to HFNC is reserved for treatment failure at 1 to 2 hours defined by hypoxia despite low-flow, increasing work of breathing or rising respiratory rate. Bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics are not routinely indicated. Feeding assessment guides transition to nasogastric feeds.
key_points: SpO2 target 90% (not 92-94%) for bronchiolitis under 12 months per RCH
Low-flow nasal prong 1-2 L/min is first-line oxygen; HFNC only for low-flow failure at 1-2 hours
Bronchodilators, corticosteroids and adrenaline nebulisers not routinely recommended
NGT feeds if intake <50% of maintenance or moderate/severe work of breathing
explanation.pearls: Do not use HFNC as a first-line escalation. RCH audit found 32% of HFNC starts were premature; low-flow held saturations in 68%.

stem: You are the paediatric intern reviewing a 3-hour-old term male on the postnatal ward. His mother has diet-controlled gestational diabetes and he weighed 4310 g at birth (95th centile). He has fed well twice on the breast since delivery. The midwife checked a pre-feed blood sugar because of his birthweight. He is pink, alert and rooting for a feed. Temperature is stable, tone is normal, and there is no jitteriness or respiratory distress. There are no other risk factors. The bedside meter reads 1.9 mmol/L; a paired laboratory sample has been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138, respiratory rate 42, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Feeding: Two effective breastfeeds since birth, latching well, no vomits, no jitters
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 1.9 mmol/L (>=2.6), paired plasma glucose pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother the reading is expected in the first 24 hours and simply repeat the pre-feed check
options.rationale: Neonatal blood glucose below 2.6 mmol/L in an at-risk infant requires action, not observation. The infant of a diabetic mother and a large-for-gestational-age infant are both listed at-risk groups by RCH and the ADIPS/NICE-derived Australian pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give an intravenous bolus of 10% dextrose 2.5 mL/kg and admit the infant to the special care nursery
options.rationale: IV dextrose bolus 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose is reserved for symptomatic hypoglycaemia (jitteriness, seizures, apnoea, poor tone) or blood glucose persistently below 1.5 mmol/L despite feeds and buccal dextrose gel. This asymptomatic infant with a modestly low reading warrants a staged feed-and-gel approach first. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give 40% dextrose buccal gel 200 mg/kg with an immediate breastfeed and recheck 30 minutes after feeding
options.rationale: For asymptomatic infants in an at-risk category with blood glucose 1.5 to 2.5 mmol/L, RCH and the Sugar Babies trial pathway recommend 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) massaged into the buccal mucosa with an immediate feed, followed by a repeat blood glucose 30 minutes after the feed. This halves the rate of admission for IV dextrose. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Commence donor expressed breast milk 20 mL/kg/day by nasogastric tube and skip the maternal breastfeed
options.rationale: Interrupting breastfeeding removes the strongest driver of postnatal glucose stabilisation. Buccal gel plus continued direct breastfeeding is preferred; NGT feeds are reserved for infants unable to feed effectively at the breast or bottle. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Wait for the paired laboratory plasma glucose result before acting because bedside meters are inaccurate
options.rationale: Point-of-care meters are known to be less accurate at extreme lows, but pathway guidance is to act on the bedside reading in a well infant while a paired sample is being processed, because delayed treatment risks neurological injury if the true glucose is low. Confirmatory sampling is drawn at the same time, not awaited before intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: The at-risk term infant with asymptomatic hypoglycaemia between 1.5 and 2.5 mmol/L should receive 40% dextrose buccal gel 200 mg/kg with an immediate feed. The Sugar Babies protocol reduces NICU admissions and preserves breastfeeding. Symptomatic infants or those with blood glucose below 1.5 mmol/L go straight to IV dextrose bolus.
key_points: Blood glucose <2.6 mmol/L in at-risk infants (IDM, LGA, SGA, preterm) triggers action
Asymptomatic 1.5-2.5 mmol/L: 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) buccal plus feed
Symptomatic OR <1.5 mmol/L: 10% dextrose IV bolus 2 mL/kg then infusion 60 mL/kg/day
Recheck glucose 30 minutes after feed following gel
explanation.pearls: Buccal 40% dextrose gel dose is 200 mg/kg = 0.5 mL/kg; maximum two doses in 24 hours before escalating to IV.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar in an emergency department. A 14-year-old girl (weight 42 kg) presents 15 minutes after eating a peanut-contaminated dessert at a birthday party. She has known peanut allergy and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy for which she takes atenolol 25 mg daily. Her mother administered her EpiPen 300 mcg intramuscularly 3 minutes ago on the way in. On arrival she has stridor, generalised urticaria and is agitated. Blood pressure is 78/44, pulse 96 with poor volume, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 92% on room air, wheeze and mild subcostal recession, and hoarse voice. She is not yet cyanotic and remains alert. A second IM adrenaline dose has just been given.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 78/44, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 92% on 15 L non-rebreather, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria, mild angioedema of lips, stridor with hoarse voice, wheeze with mild recession, cool peripheries, no cyanosis, alert and following commands
data_table.Medications: Atenolol 25 mg daily for HCM, EpiPen 300 mcg IM given by mother at scene, further 300 mcg IM given at arrival

lead_in: Despite two IM adrenaline doses she remains hypotensive and stridorous. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg over 5 minutes as second-line therapy for refractory anaphylaxis
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are adjunctive and do not treat immediate airway or circulatory compromise. Onset is delayed by hours and they have no role as second-line management of acute anaphylaxis with persistent hypotension. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intravenous chlorphenamine 10 mg over 5 minutes as second-line therapy for refractory anaphylaxis
options.rationale: Antihistamines relieve urticaria and itch but have no effect on airway obstruction or hypotension. They are not first- or second-line in refractory anaphylaxis and should never delay adrenaline infusion or fluids. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Start intravenous adrenaline infusion plus a 20 mL/kg saline bolus, and prepare glucagon for beta-blocker refractoriness
options.rationale: In refractory anaphylaxis after two IM doses, ASCIA guidance is to move to IV adrenaline infusion titrated to response (start 0.1 microgram/kg/min), give a 20 mL/kg saline bolus for hypotension, and specifically in patients on beta-blockade with refractory hypotension consider glucagon 1 to 5 mg IV (paediatric 20 to 30 microgram/kg to a maximum of 1 mg) followed by infusion because glucagon bypasses beta-adrenergic blockade via cAMP. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Administer nebulised salbutamol 5 mg on high-flow oxygen and defer any further intramuscular adrenaline dosing
options.rationale: Nebulised salbutamol may help wheeze but does not address stridor, laryngeal oedema or hypotension. Adrenaline remains the definitive agent for anaphylactic airway and circulatory compromise. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Perform emergency needle cricothyroidotomy given the stridor and hoarse voice suggesting laryngeal obstruction
options.rationale: Definitive airway is escalated when medical management fails to reverse laryngeal oedema and the airway is becoming unsustainable. Cricothyroidotomy is a last-resort rescue after failure of medical therapy and attempted intubation, not the immediate next step while pharmacological options remain available. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Refractory anaphylaxis after two doses of IM adrenaline requires escalation to IV adrenaline infusion and adjunctive volume resuscitation. Beta-blocker-treated patients may fail to respond to adrenaline, and glucagon (1 to 5 mg IV in adults; 20 to 30 microgram/kg to a max 1 mg in children) bypasses beta-adrenergic blockade via direct activation of cardiac cAMP. All patients require observation for at least 4 hours after resolution because of biphasic reaction risk.
key_points: IM adrenaline 10 mcg/kg (max 500 mcg) via ASCIA banded table is first-line; repeat every 5 min
Refractory shock or stridor: IV adrenaline infusion 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated to response
IV crystalloid 20 mL/kg bolus for hypotension, repeat as needed
Beta-blocked refractory anaphylaxis: glucagon 20-30 mcg/kg IV (max 1 mg) then infusion 5-15 mcg/min in adults
explanation.pearls: ASCIA EpiPen banded table: 150 mcg for 10-20 kg (EpiPen Jr), 300 mcg for 20+ kg (EpiPen); never use 10 mcg/kg arithmetic in a real event.

stem: You are the paediatric consultant in a community adolescent mental health clinic. A 15-year-old girl has moderate-to-severe major depressive disorder confirmed on structured assessment. Symptoms have persisted 5 months. She has completed 12 sessions of CBT with a skilled psychologist without meaningful change in her PHQ-A score (still 17). She has anhedonia, hopelessness, weight loss, and passive suicidal thoughts without plan. She has no bipolar family history, no manic features, no psychotic symptoms, and no substance use. She has never taken psychotropic medication. Baseline ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms and normal FBC, UEC, TFTs. She and her mother are willing to consider medication with regular clinic review.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 68, blood pressure 108/64, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-A 17 (moderate-severe), TSH 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count within normal limits, electrolytes within normal limits, ECG sinus rhythm QTc 410 ms
data_table.History: 12 sessions of CBT with psychologist without change, anhedonia, weight loss, passive suicidal ideation without plan, no bipolar history, no substances, no medication

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Citalopram 10 mg once daily titrated to 20 mg once daily over 2 weeks with weekly monitoring for adverse effects
options.rationale: Citalopram is not first-line for adolescent depression in Australia. RANZCP guidance and TGA-approved indications point to fluoxetine as the first-line SSRI with the strongest paediatric evidence base and TGA approval for use in this age group. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

options.text: Sertraline 25 mg once daily titrated to 50 mg once daily over 2 weeks with weekly monitoring for adverse effects
options.rationale: Sertraline is used as second-line in adolescents when fluoxetine has failed or is not tolerated. Fluoxetine is preferred first-line because of the strongest paediatric RCT evidence (TADS) and TGA registration. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

options.text: Venlafaxine XR 37.5 mg once daily titrated to 75 mg once daily over 2 weeks with weekly monitoring
options.rationale: Venlafaxine is not first-line in adolescents because of higher rates of hypertension, discontinuation symptoms and increased signal for suicidal ideation in paediatric RCTs. It is reserved for treatment-resistant cases with specialist supervision. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

options.text: Fluoxetine 10 mg once daily titrated to 20 mg once daily over 1 to 2 weeks with weekly monitoring for adverse effects
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is the first-line SSRI for adolescent moderate-severe major depressive disorder after failure of an adequate psychological therapy trial. TADS demonstrated superiority of fluoxetine plus CBT over either alone and TGA registration supports use in this age group. Starting at 10 mg daily and titrating to 20 mg after 1 to 2 weeks reduces initial activation. Weekly monitoring for suicidal ideation is required in the first 4 to 6 weeks per RANZCP guidance. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

options.text: Mirtazapine 15 mg nightly titrated to 30 mg nightly over 2 weeks with weekly monitoring for adverse effects
options.rationale: Mirtazapine has limited paediatric RCT data and is not endorsed as first-line in adolescents. Weight-gain and sedation side-effect profile also disfavours it in an adolescent with existing weight loss where activation is desired. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

explanation.summary: Fluoxetine is the first-line SSRI for adolescent major depressive disorder failing an adequate trial of evidence-based psychological therapy such as CBT or IPT-A. TADS demonstrated combination of fluoxetine plus CBT is more effective than either alone. Weekly monitoring for treatment-emergent suicidal ideation is mandated for at least 4 weeks after starting. Full antidepressant effect is assessed at 4 to 6 weeks.
key_points: Adolescent MDD first-line pharmacotherapy: fluoxetine 10 mg titrated to 20 mg
Combine with evidence-based CBT or IPT-A (superiority over either alone in TADS)
Weekly monitoring for suicidal ideation for first 4-6 weeks after starting SSRI
Sertraline is second-line adolescent SSRI; escitalopram third-line specialist choice
explanation.pearls: TADS trial: fluoxetine + CBT 71% response, fluoxetine alone 61%, CBT alone 43%, placebo 35% at 12 weeks. Combination is preferred whenever both are available.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar assessing a 5-month-old infant brought to the emergency department by his mother, who says he rolled off the bed 30 minutes ago. He is now crying but consolable. On examination there is bruising over the right cheek and behind the left ear, a small oval bruise on the anterior chest wall, and swelling of the right thigh with reluctance to bear weight on that leg. A brief screen shows he cannot yet roll from prone to supine or supine to prone. The mother appears anxious and the father sits quietly separated from the family. Radiograph of the right femur shows a mid-shaft spiral fracture. There is no prior child protection concern documented in the state health record.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bruises over right cheek, behind left ear, anterior chest oval bruise; right thigh swelling with reluctance to bear weight, moves other limbs symmetrically; anterior fontanelle soft and flat; developmentally cannot yet roll
data_table.Investigations: Right femur radiograph shows mid-shaft spiral fracture, full blood count within normal limits, coagulation profile within normal limits, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Reassure the family and apply a temporary femoral splint with orthopaedic fracture-clinic review at 24 hours
options.rationale: The pattern here (bruising in a non-mobile infant, torso and head sites, and a long-bone spiral fracture with a history discordant with the child's developmental stage) meets multiple red flags for inflicted injury. Discharging without paediatric admission, safeguarding involvement and full skeletal survey would fail the child. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Test for osteogenesis imperfecta and copper deficiency before considering any child protection notification
options.rationale: While metabolic and skeletal disorders (osteogenesis imperfecta, copper deficiency) are on the differential, they are investigated in parallel with, not before, mandatory child protection notification and admission. The child's protection cannot wait for a genetic workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Send the infant home with mother once the femoral splint is applied and give safety-net telephone advice only
options.rationale: Discharge home is unsafe when inflicted injury is suspected. The child requires medical admission for full evaluation, protective placement decisions and clarity around safe custody. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Ask the mother to leave the room and ask the father directly whether he shook or dropped the child in question
options.rationale: Confronting either parent alone in the emergency department without a structured multidisciplinary approach can compromise the child's safety, the investigation, and the parent's rights. Assessment is done in a structured setting through the child protection service. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Admit for evaluation, notify state child protection today, and arrange skeletal survey plus CT head plus eye review
options.rationale: This infant has multiple red flags for inflicted injury: bruising in a pre-mobile infant, high-risk anatomical sites (torso, ears, head), a long-bone fracture at an age when the child cannot yet self-mobilise, and a history discordant with developmental stage. Australian and RCH guidance mandates admission, statutory notification to the state child protection service by any doctor as a mandatory reporter, and a full skeletal survey in infants under 2 years, with non-contrast CT head and dilated ophthalmology examination to look for occult subdural haemorrhage and retinal haemorrhages. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: Bruising in a non-mobile infant, torso and head site bruising, and long-bone fracture with a history inconsistent with the child's developmental stage are strong indicators of inflicted injury. Immediate steps are admission for a safe environment, mandatory statutory notification to the state child protection service by any doctor, and a comprehensive investigation cascade (full skeletal survey, non-contrast CT head, dilated ophthalmology for retinal haemorrhage). Alternative explanations are investigated in parallel, not before, safeguarding.
key_points: TEN-4 FACESp bruising rule: bruises to torso, ear, neck under 4 years or any bruise in infant <4 months warrants NAI evaluation
Full skeletal survey mandatory in <2 years with suspected inflicted injury
Non-contrast CT head and dilated ophthalmology exam to detect occult subdural + retinal haemorrhages
Mandatory reporter notification is a legal duty; not dependent on caseworker approval
explanation.pearls: Fractures with high specificity for inflicted injury include metaphyseal corner (classic metaphyseal lesion), posterior rib, scapular, spinous process and sternal fractures.

subtopic_detail: Neonatal seizure with normal blood glucose
stem: You are the neonatal registrar called to a term-born day 2 male infant on the postnatal ward. Birthweight 3410 g, Apgar 9 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, mother well and afebrile, no perinatal risk factors identified, breastfeeding established. The nurse describes a 90-second episode of tonic-clonic movement of the left arm with lip smacking, apnoea to SpO2 of 82%, and eye deviation to the left. Postictally he is drowsy but rousable. Bedside blood glucose is 3.4 mmol/L, capillary blood gas is normal, temperature is 36.9 degrees Celsius, no history of maternal opioid or SSRI exposure. His father reports that his own brother had recurrent neonatal seizures that resolved by 6 months without long-term epilepsy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, respiratory rate 42, SpO2 98% on room air post-event, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Anterior fontanelle soft flat, tone normal, moro symmetric, no dysmorphic features, no skin lesions on Wood's lamp, cord well healed, no organomegaly, no bruises
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 3.4 mmol/L (>2.6), capillary blood gas within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), calcium ionised 1.20 mmol/L (1.10-1.30), magnesium 0.82 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145)
data_table.History: Term uncomplicated pregnancy, no maternal opioid or SSRI exposure, family history of paternal uncle with self-resolving neonatal seizures

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral phenytoin 5 mg/kg every 12 hours and discharge to the postnatal ward on standard observations
options.rationale: Oral phenytoin absorption in neonates is erratic and phenytoin is not first-line for neonatal seizure. Discharge to routine observation misses the essential workup for infection and structural cause. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

options.text: Reassure the family this is likely jitteriness given the normal blood glucose and observe on the postnatal ward
options.rationale: This event is not consistent with benign neonatal jitteriness: jitteriness is stimulus-sensitive, stoppable with limb hold, and lacks eye deviation, apnoea and postictal drowsiness. The presentation is a focal clonic seizure requiring urgent workup. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

options.text: Give intramuscular vitamin K 1 mg and observe on the postnatal ward for further seizure activity before any workup
options.rationale: Vitamin K is important for haemostasis but does not treat or diagnose neonatal seizure. Deferring workup means missing time-critical causes such as meningitis or hypoglycaemia recurrence. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

options.text: Transfer to special care nursery for septic screen, empirical antibiotics plus aciclovir, EEG, MRI and metabolic panel
options.rationale: A term neonate with a focal clonic seizure of this description and a family history of self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy (KCNQ2 phenotype) requires broad emergency workup because early identification of infection (bacterial meningitis, HSV encephalitis), stroke, structural brain lesion, and inborn errors of metabolism (pyridoxine-dependent seizure, urea cycle defect) is time-critical. RCH and PSANZ neonatal seizure guidance mandate full septic screen with lumbar puncture, empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics plus aciclovir, EEG, cranial imaging and metabolic workup including a pyridoxine trial. First-line acute anticonvulsant is phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

options.text: Perform a diagnostic lumbar puncture only and manage empirically as bacterial meningitis given the family history
options.rationale: A single positive family history is not diagnostic and the workup must be broader; anticonvulsant plans, imaging, metabolic testing and cover for HSV encephalitis must accompany the septic workup. Narrow investigation risks missing critical causes. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

explanation.summary: A term neonate with a focal seizure and normal blood glucose requires urgent transfer to a special care nursery for broad workup: full septic screen including lumbar puncture, empirical antibiotics plus aciclovir for HSV encephalitis, urgent EEG, cranial imaging (ultrasound then MRI), metabolic panel including plasma amino acids, ammonia, lactate, acylcarnitine profile and a pyridoxine trial. First-line anticonvulsant for recurrent seizure is phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV. Family history of self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy is a diagnosis of exclusion after infection, structural and metabolic causes are excluded.
key_points: Neonatal seizure with normal BSL: broad workup including septic screen with LP, empirical Abx + aciclovir, EEG, MRI, metabolic panel including pyridoxine trial
First-line acute anticonvulsant: phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV; second-line phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV
HSV encephalitis in neonate can present with focal seizure without skin lesions; empirical aciclovir is mandatory until PCR back
Self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy (KCNQ2) is a diagnosis of exclusion; suspicion warrants genetic panel
explanation.pearls: Pyridoxine-dependent seizure responds to 100 mg IV pyridoxine given during EEG-monitored administration; presence of seizure cessation is diagnostic and requires life-long supplementation.

subtopic_detail: Newly diagnosed ITP with wet purpura
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a previously well 4-year-old boy brought by his mother because he woke this morning with numerous small purple spots on his legs and trunk, and this afternoon developed a nosebleed that lasted 20 minutes needing pressure. Two weeks ago he had a viral upper respiratory tract infection which has resolved. He looks systemically well, active, and afebrile.

Examination reveals scattered petechiae over the trunk and limbs, three small ecchymoses on the shins, blood in the nares and dry blood at the lips, mild bleeding gums when he yawns. Abdomen is soft with no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no bone tenderness.

Full blood count: haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140), white cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (4-12), neutrophils 3.6 x10^9/L, lymphocytes 4.0 x10^9/L, platelets 6 x10^9/L (150-400). Film shows large platelets, no blasts. Coagulation profile normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 100/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L (110-140), WCC 8.2 x10^9/L (4-12), platelets 6 x10^9/L (150-400), film large platelets no blasts, coags normal
data_table.Exam: petechiae, bruises, active epistaxis, bleeding gums, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge home with observation only, arrange platelet count in 48 hours, avoid contact sports and NSAIDs
options.rationale: Observation alone applies to dry purpura (skin bruising and petechiae only) in a well child; active mucosal bleeding (wet purpura) shifts management towards pharmacological intervention due to intracranial bleed risk. (Source: RCH ITP)

options.text: Admit and administer intravenous immunoglobulin 0.8 g/kg as a single dose with paracetamol pre-medication
options.rationale: Newly diagnosed ITP with wet purpura (mucosal bleeding, epistaxis, gum bleed) plus platelets under 20 x10^9/L warrants urgent platelet elevation; IVIG 0.8 to 1 g/kg gives fastest platelet rise (typically within 24 to 48 h) with a favourable side-effect profile in children. (Source: RCH ITP)

options.text: Transfuse a single unit of pooled platelets to raise the count acutely and prevent further mucosal bleeding
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion in ITP is generally ineffective because transfused platelets are destroyed by autoantibody; reserve for life-threatening bleeding as a bridging measure with immunoglobulin and steroid together. (Source: RCH ITP)

options.text: Perform bone marrow aspirate today to exclude leukaemia before commencing any specific therapy for this presentation
options.rationale: Bone marrow aspirate is not required when the presentation is classic ITP (isolated thrombocytopenia, well child, no atypical features on film); it may be done later only if the response to first-line therapy is atypical. (Source: RCH ITP)

options.text: Commence prednisolone 4 mg/kg daily for 4 days without further investigation and review platelet count at day 7
options.rationale: High-dose oral steroid is a valid alternative but is slower to raise platelets than IVIG and requires excluding malignancy on film beforehand; IVIG is preferred in active mucosal bleeding for speed of response. (Source: RCH ITP)

explanation.summary: ITP with wet purpura in a child (active mucosal bleeding) and platelets under 20 x10^9/L is a treatment indication because of the small but serious risk of intracranial haemorrhage. IVIG 0.8 to 1 g/kg is first-line for speed of platelet rise. Dry purpura in a well child with isolated thrombocytopenia may be observed. Bone marrow aspirate is not required if the film is otherwise normal.
key_points: Dry purpura, well child: observe
Wet purpura or platelets <20: treat (IVIG first-line for speed)
Steroid alternative (prednisolone 4 mg/kg/d x 4d) if IVIG contraindicated
Platelet transfusion only for life-threatening bleed as bridge
explanation.pearls: Paediatric ICH risk in ITP is 0.1 to 1%; wet purpura triples risk. Avoid IM injections, NSAIDs, aspirin, and contact sport while count is low.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8-year-old girl 6 hours into treatment of new type 1 diabetes with severe diabetic ketoacidosis. On admission her pH was 7.02, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, glucose 32 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L. She received a 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus and has been on 0.9 percent saline with potassium at maintenance plus 5 percent deficit replacement over 48 hours, with an insulin infusion at 0.05 unit/kg/hour. Her glucose has fallen from 32 to 14 mmol/L. She had been chatty and reading her book.

At this review she complains of a new headache, has vomited once, and is now more drowsy (GCS 12: E3V4M5). Blood pressure has risen from 108/64 to 138/86 and her pulse has fallen from 118 to 68. There is no papilloedema visible but pupils are equal and reactive. Her most recent electrolytes show sodium 138, glucose 12, and pH 7.22.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 68 (was 118), blood pressure 138/86 (was 108/64), respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Progress: 6 hours DKA Rx, glucose 32 to 12, pH 7.02 to 7.22
data_table.Neuro: new headache, one vomit, GCS 12 (E3V4M5), pupils equal and reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion to 0.1 unit/kg/hour and add dextrose 10 percent to accelerate resolution of acidosis and ketogenesis
options.rationale: The concern here is cerebral oedema, not persistent acidosis; increasing insulin without addressing the neurological signs is dangerous. Ongoing rehydration and steady insulin at 0.05 unit/kg/hour is appropriate provided glucose fall is not too fast. (Source: RCH DKA)

options.text: Administer another 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus to correct hypovolaemia given her drowsiness and headache
options.rationale: Additional aggressive rehydration risks worsening cerebral oedema; total fluid rate should be reduced by one-third when oedema is suspected. Rising BP and falling pulse are Cushing physiology, not hypovolaemia. (Source: RCH DKA)

options.text: Give 3 percent saline 3 mL/kg over 15 minutes or mannitol 0.5 g/kg, reduce fluid rate by one-third, arrange CT after treatment
options.rationale: Bradycardia and rising BP with headache, vomiting and depressed conscious level are Muir/Glaser cerebral oedema criteria requiring immediate hyperosmolar therapy; 3 percent saline 3 mL/kg IV (or mannitol 0.5 g/kg) is first-line before any imaging. (Source: RCH DKA)

options.text: Arrange an immediate CT head to confirm cerebral oedema before commencing any specific therapy for the neurological deterioration
options.rationale: Treatment must not be delayed for imaging when cerebral oedema is clinically apparent; hyperosmolar therapy is given first, then CT once stabilised (or if there is no response). (Source: RCH DKA)

options.text: Give sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg IV to correct the residual metabolic acidosis and improve cerebral perfusion during recovery
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA except in life-threatening hyperkalaemia because it worsens cerebral oedema and paradoxical CNS acidosis. (Source: RCH DKA)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of DKA mortality in children. Risk factors include younger age, severe acidosis at presentation, higher urea, low PaCO2, and treatment with bicarbonate or excess fluid. Warning signs (Muir/Glaser): headache, recurrent vomiting, drowsiness, incontinence, hypertension with bradycardia, cranial nerve palsy, abnormal breathing pattern. Treatment is immediate hyperosmolar therapy (3 percent saline 3 mL/kg over 15 minutes or mannitol 0.5 g/kg over 15 minutes), reduce fluid rate, elevate head, and CT after stabilisation.
key_points: Cushing physiology (hypertension + bradycardia) with headache/vomiting equals cerebral oedema
Treat with 3% saline 3 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 g/kg IV before CT
Reduce fluid rate by one-third; avoid rapid glucose fall (>5 mmol/L/h)
Avoid bicarbonate; add dextrose when glucose <14 to prevent hypoglycaemia
explanation.pearls: Fluid deficit calculation in paediatric DKA: assume 5 to 7% dehydration in DKA, 10% in HHS; replace over 48 hours plus maintenance. Two-bag system (0.9% saline vs 0.9% saline plus 10% dextrose) allows steady glucose fall.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9-month-old boy who has had a temperature of 39 to 40 degrees Celsius for 6 days. He has been listless, refused feeds intermittently, and had a single loose stool this morning. On examination today: irritable but consolable, a diffuse maculopapular rash across the trunk that has been present 3 days, mild bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, dry cracked lips without oral ulcers, no lymphadenopathy, no peripheral changes. He has not had a coryzal illness. No known unwell contacts.

Bloods: haemoglobin 96 g/L (105-135), white cell count 18.2 x10^9/L (5-15), neutrophils 12.6 x10^9/L, platelets 512 x10^9/L (150-450), CRP 118 mg/L (below 5), ESR 82 mm/h, albumin 24 g/L (35-50), ALT 88 U/L (below 40), sodium 132 mmol/L. Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria. Blood cultures at 24 h are negative. Chest X-ray is clear.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 96 g/L, WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, platelets 512 x10^9/L, CRP 118 mg/L (<5), ESR 82 mm/h, albumin 24 g/L (35-50), ALT 88 U/L (<40)
data_table.Urine: sterile pyuria on dipstick and microscopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start high-dose oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily for 5 days for a suspected autoimmune inflammatory process while awaiting further tests
options.rationale: Steroids are second-line in Kawasaki (used with IVIG in high-risk or IVIG-resistant cases per the Kobayashi score), not first-line monotherapy; IVIG remains the primary therapy. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)

options.text: Continue empirical IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily and repeat sepsis workup at 48 hours if fever persists before considering IVIG
options.rationale: Delaying IVIG beyond day 10 of illness increases coronary artery aneurysm risk; if incomplete Kawasaki criteria are met, treatment should not await further sepsis workup. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol pending viral swab result and community follow-up in 3 to 5 days to reassess response
options.rationale: A well-appearing infant with 6 days of fever and inflammatory picture is unsafe to discharge without excluding Kawasaki disease; missed cases risk coronary aneurysms. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)

options.text: Arrange echocardiography now, treat as incomplete Kawasaki disease with IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours and aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg/day
options.rationale: Prolonged fever with only two of five principal Kawasaki criteria (rash and non-purulent conjunctivitis) in an infant with supportive laboratory findings (raised CRP, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria, transaminitis, anaemia) meets AHA incomplete Kawasaki criteria; treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin, and echocardiography documents coronary status. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)

options.text: Add IV vancomycin and admit for observation; hold immunoglobulin until infection is definitely excluded on microbiology
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone are insufficient if incomplete Kawasaki criteria are met and delay definitive therapy; concurrent bacterial infection does not exclude Kawasaki disease. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease diagnosis requires 5 or more days of fever plus 4 of 5 principal criteria (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes, polymorphous rash, peripheral extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy). Incomplete Kawasaki is diagnosed with 2 or 3 principal criteria plus supportive laboratory or echocardiographic findings, particularly in infants under 12 months (highest risk group for coronary aneurysms). Treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin, with echocardiography to document coronary status.
key_points: Classic KD: fever >=5 days plus 4 of 5 principal criteria
Incomplete KD: fever >=5 days plus 2 or 3 criteria plus supportive labs
Infants <12 months at highest risk for coronary aneurysms; low threshold to treat
Treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg single dose + aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg/d (some centres 30 to 80)
explanation.pearls: AHA supportive lab criteria for incomplete KD (at least 3 of): anaemia for age, platelets over 450 after day 7, albumin under 30, ALT elevated, WCC over 15, sterile pyuria. Kobayashi score identifies IVIG-resistant patients for adjunctive steroid.

stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a 60-hour-old term baby born at 39+2 weeks by normal vaginal delivery, birth weight 3.4 kg. Mother has blood group O positive with anti-A antibodies. Baby was noted to be visibly jaundiced by 24 hours of age. He has been feeding briefly but not vigorously, passing 3 wet nappies over the past 12 hours, and lost 6 percent of birth weight.

Baby is now lethargic with a poor cry and reduced tone. Cephalocaudal jaundice extends to soles of feet. He is afebrile, saturating well in air, no bruising, no cephalohaematoma. There is no organomegaly. Bilirubin at admission was 340 micromol/L, now at 60 hours it is 512 micromol/L. Direct antiglobulin test is positive. Baby's blood group is A positive. Reticulocyte count is 8 percent (0.5 to 2). Haemoglobin 128 g/L (145 to 225 at 24 hours). He is on triple-bank intensive phototherapy for the past 4 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 158, blood pressure 62/38, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: total bilirubin 512 umol/L (age 60h phototherapy line ~380, exchange line ~430), DAT positive, retic 8%, Hb 128 g/L, ABO incompatibility
data_table.Rx so far: triple bank intensive phototherapy 4 hours, IV fluids commenced

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue intensive phototherapy alone and repeat serum bilirubin in 6 hours before deciding on exchange transfusion
options.rationale: Bilirubin above the exchange transfusion threshold at 60 hours with clinical features of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (lethargy, poor tone, poor cry) mandates immediate exchange, not further observation on phototherapy alone. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Stop phototherapy to prevent riboflavin depletion and give oral ursodeoxycholic acid 20 mg/kg/day until bilirubin falls
options.rationale: Stopping phototherapy allows further bilirubin rise; ursodeoxycholic acid has no role in unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Continued intensive phototherapy alongside exchange is standard. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Give a top-up transfusion of packed red cells 10 mL/kg to correct the anaemia, then observe with phototherapy for 12 hours
options.rationale: Simple top-up transfusion does not remove circulating bilirubin or antibody; only exchange transfusion clears both and is required at this bilirubin level with encephalopathy. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Administer intravenous phenobarbital 15 mg/kg loading dose to induce hepatic conjugation of unconjugated bilirubin
options.rationale: Phenobarbital has a slow onset (days) and no role in acute severe hyperbilirubinaemia with encephalopathy; immediate mechanical clearance by exchange is required. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Prepare for double-volume exchange transfusion urgently while continuing intensive phototherapy and giving IVIG 0.5 g/kg for immune haemolysis
options.rationale: Bilirubin over the exchange line at 60 hours with signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy in a baby with immune haemolysis requires urgent double-volume exchange transfusion; IVIG 0.5 g/kg over 2 hours may reduce need for exchange in immune haemolytic disease. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Severe neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia with acute bilirubin encephalopathy is a neurological emergency. Immune haemolytic causes (Rh, ABO, minor blood group incompatibility) have a positive DAT and elevated reticulocyte count. When bilirubin exceeds the exchange transfusion threshold on the age-specific nomogram, or when signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy appear (lethargy, hypotonia, poor feed, high-pitched cry, opisthotonos, seizures), immediate double-volume exchange transfusion is indicated with concurrent intensive phototherapy. IVIG 0.5 g/kg reduces need for exchange in immune haemolysis.
key_points: Bilirubin above exchange line OR any acute encephalopathy signs equals immediate exchange
IVIG 0.5 g/kg over 2 hours in immune haemolysis may reduce need for exchange
Continue intensive phototherapy throughout
Isovolumetric exchange with double blood volume (~160 mL/kg)
explanation.pearls: NICE and RCH nomograms differ slightly; the current RCH exchange line at 60 hours for a well term baby is roughly 430 micromol/L (lower with haemolysis or prematurity). Escalate immediately if encephalopathy signs present regardless of exact number.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8-year-old girl who presented three weeks ago with palpable purpura over her buttocks and lower limbs, symmetrical ankle and knee joint swelling, and colicky abdominal pain. She was diagnosed with IgA vasculitis (previously called Henoch-Schonlein purpura). Her purpura and abdominal pain resolved with paracetamol; joint swelling settled.

Weekly urinalysis for surveillance now shows blood 3+ and protein 3+. Her spot urine protein/creatinine ratio is 320 mg/mmol (below 20). Serum albumin is 24 g/L (35 to 50), creatinine 78 umol/L (30 to 60 for her age), estimated GFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure is 132/86 which is above the 95th centile for age, sex, and height. She has periorbital and pretibial oedema. Complement C3 and C4 are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 132/86 (>95th centile), respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: creatinine 78 umol/L (30-60), eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m2, albumin 24 g/L (35-50), C3 normal, C4 normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to paediatric nephrology urgently and arrange renal biopsy plus commence oral prednisolone pending histology and steroid-based induction
options.rationale: IgA vasculitis nephritis with nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension and reduced eGFR requires urgent nephrology referral, renal biopsy for prognostic and treatment classification (Oxford/ISKDC), and empirical steroid therapy is often started pending biopsy result. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)

options.text: Continue weekly urine surveillance for another 6 months and reassess if proteinuria persists or worsens further
options.rationale: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with reduced GFR and hypertension in IgA vasculitis nephritis requires renal biopsy and specialist input, not further observation which risks progression. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)

options.text: Start oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg 8-hourly empirically for possible post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis pending ASOT results
options.rationale: Normal complement and preceding IgA vasculitis do not fit post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis; antibiotics are not indicated and delay appropriate immunosuppression assessment. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)

options.text: Restrict dietary salt and fluid and reassess urinalysis and blood pressure in 4 weeks at the local General practice for review
options.rationale: Dietary measures alone are insufficient for nephritic-nephrotic syndrome with rising creatinine; specialist assessment and biopsy are needed within days, not weeks. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)

options.text: Commence enalapril 0.1 mg/kg daily for the hypertension and continue outpatient monitoring monthly without further investigation
options.rationale: ACE inhibitor is a reasonable adjunct but insufficient alone with nephrotic range proteinuria and reduced GFR; biopsy and immunosuppression assessment are the priority. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis nephritis presents as haematuria and/or proteinuria in the weeks to months after the acute vasculitic illness. Weekly urinalysis for 6 to 12 months detects it early. Indications for renal biopsy and nephrology referral include nephrotic range proteinuria (uPCR over 200 mg/mmol), impaired renal function, persistent hypertension, or persistent macroscopic haematuria and proteinuria beyond 3 months. Steroid-based induction is standard for significant nephritis, guided by biopsy histology.
key_points: Weekly urinalysis for 6 to 12 months after acute IgA vasculitis
Biopsy triggers: nephrotic proteinuria, reduced GFR, hypertension, persistent haematuria+proteinuria
Empiric steroids often started pending biopsy
Preventive steroids do NOT prevent nephritis (KIGARI trial)
explanation.pearls: ISKDC classification I to VI grades severity by crescents; over 50% crescents or focal segmental glomerulosclerosis has worse prognosis. Renal outcomes are the main long-term determinant, with 1 to 5% risk of ESKD in nephritic cases.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to ED for a 3-year-old boy with 4 days of fever, sore throat, and increasing neck stiffness. Today he has developed drooling, refuses to swallow, and holds his neck extended. He is anxious, sits upright on his father's lap, muffled voice, mild stridor at rest, no drooling on arrival. Temperature 39.4, pulse 148, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 96 percent on room air.

He will not open his mouth for examination. There is a visible swelling in the posterior pharyngeal wall on limited view. There is tender cervical lymphadenopathy. Bloods: WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 186 mg/L. Neck lateral X-ray shows widening of the prevertebral soft tissues at C3 to 5 to greater than half the vertebral body width. Blood cultures have been taken.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Exam: sits upright, muffled voice, mild stridor, neck extended, will not open mouth, tender cervical nodes
data_table.Bloods and imaging: WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 186 mg/L (<5), lateral neck XR prevertebral soft tissue widening C3-5

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Perform bedside incision and drainage with local anaesthesia in ED before transfer to reduce ongoing airway swelling and time to source control
options.rationale: Bedside drainage of a paediatric retropharyngeal abscess risks catastrophic airway loss and aspiration; drainage is done in theatre with definitive airway. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)

options.text: Cannulate immediately in ED, take blood cultures, and give IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg and metronidazole 15 mg/kg before ENT is contacted
options.rationale: Cannulation may cause the child to cry and lose the airway; treatment in a compromised paediatric airway starts with keeping the child calm and moving to a controlled theatre environment, then antibiotics and drainage. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)
