options.text: Keep child calm, call ENT and paediatric anaesthetics urgently, transfer to theatre for controlled inhalational induction and drainage
options.rationale: Retropharyngeal abscess with airway compromise (stridor, muffled voice, drooling, opisthotonos) in a young child requires controlled airway management in theatre with senior ENT and paediatric anaesthetics; distress can precipitate obstruction. Drainage and IV antibiotics follow airway control. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)

options.text: Nebulise adrenaline 5 mg and give IV dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg for stridor, then arrange contrast CT neck once he settles
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone are for croup, not deep neck space infection; CT is helpful but only after airway assessment in theatre because a child with mild stridor at rest can decompensate on scanner. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)

options.text: Perform urgent rapid sequence intubation in the ED using ketamine and rocuronium to secure the airway then arrange transfer
options.rationale: Emergency intubation of a paediatric distorted airway in ED risks catastrophic failure; the standard is inhalational induction in theatre by paediatric anaesthetics with ENT available for surgical airway backup. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)

explanation.summary: Retropharyngeal abscess presents in toddlers as fever, sore throat, drooling, muffled voice, neck extension or torticollis, with lateral neck film showing prevertebral widening (over half vertebral body width at C2, over one vertebral body at C6). Management prioritises airway: keep the child calm, escalate to paediatric anaesthetics and ENT, controlled inhalational induction in theatre, then drainage and IV antibiotics.
key_points: Airway first: keep calm, do not agitate, escalate to ENT and paediatric anaesthetics
Controlled inhalational induction in theatre, NOT RSI in ED
Empiric IV ceftriaxone plus clindamycin (or metronidazole) after airway secured
Contrast CT for surgical planning after airway assessment
explanation.pearls: Distinguish from epiglottitis (rapid onset, tripod, drooling, no torticollis) and croup (barking cough, no drooling). Retropharyngeal lateral film sign: prevertebral soft tissue >7 mm at C2 or >14 mm at C6 (or >1x vertebral body width).

subtopic_detail: Chronic functional constipation with faecal impaction
stem:
You are the general paediatric registrar reviewing a 5-year-old boy in clinic with an 18-month history of infrequent hard stools (1 to 2 per week), painful defaecation, stool withholding behaviour, and 4 months of daily faecal soiling. His parents describe him passing large stools that block the toilet. He has been drinking adequate fluids, has a varied diet, and has no red flags on history (no delayed meconium, no bilious vomiting, no failure to thrive, normal spine and back examination, normal anal position).

On examination he is well grown at 50th centile for weight and height, abdomen is soft with a large firm mass in the left lower quadrant, no visible pelvic organs. Anal inspection is normal, no anal tags or fissures. His parents have tried lactulose, senna, and dietary fibre without meaningful improvement over 3 months.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 96/60, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Exam: large firm faecal mass LLQ, normal spine, normal anal position, no fissure or tag
data_table.History: 18-month course, hard weekly stools, withholding, 4 months daily soiling, prior lactulose and senna failed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Commence high-dose oral macrogol (PEG) for 3 days for faecal disimpaction, then maintenance macrogol titrated to soft daily stools
options.rationale: Chronic functional constipation with faecal impaction requires disimpaction with high-dose oral macrogol (1 to 1.5 g/kg/day for 3 days) then maintenance dosing titrated to soft daily stools; parent education and behavioural toileting are essential adjuncts. (Source: RCH Constipation)

options.text: Perform a rectal biopsy urgently to exclude Hirschsprung disease before commencing any further laxative therapy for this child
options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease presents in early infancy with delayed meconium and typically failure to thrive; a well-grown 5-year-old with classic functional constipation history does not warrant biopsy. (Source: RCH Constipation)

options.text: Perform daily bisacodyl suppositories at home for two weeks followed by oral senna as long-term maintenance therapy for this child
options.rationale: Rectal treatments are more distressing for children and less effective than oral macrogol for both disimpaction and maintenance; oral therapy is first-line unless oral is not tolerated. (Source: RCH Constipation)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for an ACE (antegrade continence enema) procedure given his failure of prior conservative therapy over months
options.rationale: ACE is reserved for refractory constipation after optimised medical therapy including adequate disimpaction and maintenance macrogol with behavioural support has failed. (Source: RCH Constipation)

options.text: Prescribe a lactose-free diet trial for 4 weeks with reassessment because cow milk protein allergy is a leading cause of functional constipation
options.rationale: Cow milk protein allergy contributes in a small subset (particularly infants) but is not the first-line intervention in a 5-year-old with classic functional constipation; disimpaction and maintenance is standard. (Source: RCH Constipation)

explanation.summary: Chronic functional constipation with faecal impaction in children is managed by (1) disimpaction with high-dose oral macrogol (PEG) for 3 to 7 days, (2) maintenance macrogol titrated to soft daily stools continued for at least 2 to 6 months, (3) toileting behavioural strategy (sit after meals, footstool, reward chart), and (4) parent education. Red flags requiring further workup include delayed meconium, failure to thrive, abnormal spine or perianal examination, or onset before 1 month of age.
key_points: Disimpaction: macrogol 1 to 1.5 g/kg/day PO for 3 days (some centres up to 7)
Maintenance: macrogol titrated to soft daily stool for months, not weeks
Toilet behavioural strategy is essential alongside laxatives
Rectal treatments only if oral fails or refused
explanation.pearls: Movicol Junior (macrogol) sachets: 1 to 2 sachets/day maintenance; 4 to 12 sachets/day for disimpaction depending on age. Do not stop maintenance for at least 2 months of regular painless stools then wean slowly to avoid relapse.

subtopic_detail: Term neonate with clinical instability at 6 hours of life
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6 hour old term neonate born by spontaneous vaginal birth to a mother with prolonged rupture of membranes at 22 hours. GBS status was unknown and no intrapartum antibiotics were given. The baby is now tachypnoeic at 78, has grunting, and central capillary refill of 4 seconds. Rectal temperature is 35.6 degrees. Feeding has been poor. There is no meningism assessable. Weight is 3.2 kg.

The consultant is on their way and asks you to start initial management now.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 172, blood pressure 46/28, respiratory rate 78 with grunting, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 35.6 degrees Celsius rectal, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Bloods: blood cultures drawn, glucose 2.4 mmol/L (2.6-6.0), lactate 4.8 mmol/L (under 2.0), FBC and CRP pending
data_table.Imaging: chest X-ray requested, cranial ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen and initial supportive step?

options.text: IV vancomycin 15 mg per kg 12 hourly plus IV meropenem 20 mg per kg 8 hourly as broad spectrum first choice
options.rationale: Vancomycin plus meropenem is not first line for early-onset neonatal sepsis; ben-pen plus gent covers GBS, Listeria, and gram negatives adequately for empirical therapy in the first 72 hours. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Sepsis Guideline)

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 60 mg per kg 12 hourly plus IV gentamicin 5 mg per kg daily, and give 10 percent dextrose bolus
options.rationale: Australian neonatal early-onset sepsis empirical regimen is benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin; dextrose 10 percent 2 mL per kg IV corrects the hypoglycaemia in this clinically unstable neonate. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Sepsis Guideline)

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 50 mg per kg once daily monotherapy pending cultures and cerebrospinal fluid results
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates because it displaces bilirubin and precipitates with calcium containing fluids causing lethal reactions; ben-pen plus gent is standard. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Sepsis Guideline)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 30 mg per kg 8 hourly and observation on the postnatal ward without any IV access placed
options.rationale: Oral therapy is unsafe in a clinically unstable neonate with shock features; IV antibiotics after blood cultures are mandatory. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Sepsis Guideline)

options.text: IV cefotaxime 50 mg per kg 8 hourly alone, hold benzylpenicillin until CSF confirmed and no cover for Listeria added
options.rationale: Cefotaxime alone lacks reliable Listeria cover; ben-pen (or ampicillin) is required in the neonatal empirical regimen. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Sepsis Guideline)

explanation.summary: Neonatal early-onset sepsis is treated empirically with benzylpenicillin (or ampicillin) plus gentamicin after blood cultures, covering GBS, Listeria, E. coli, and other gram negatives. Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates and hypoglycaemia is corrected with 10 percent dextrose 2 mL per kg IV bolus. Lumbar puncture is performed after stabilisation, not before. Duration is 7 to 10 days if bacteraemia proven, longer for meningitis.
key_points: Empirical regimen: benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin IV
Avoid ceftriaxone in neonates (bilirubin displacement, calcium precipitation)
Correct hypoglycaemia with 10% dextrose 2 mL per kg IV
Lumbar puncture after stabilisation, not before, in unstable neonate
explanation.pearls: RCH Melbourne dosing: benzylpenicillin 60 mg per kg IV 12 hourly first week of life, gentamicin 5 mg per kg IV once daily; add IV aciclovir 20 mg per kg 8 hourly if HSV features (vesicles, seizures, hepatitis).

subtopic_detail: Impending respiratory failure on high flow oxygen
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in ED reviewing a 4 month old boy with 3 days of coryza and cough, now with feeding failure and increased work of breathing. He is on humidified high flow nasal cannulae at 2 L per kg per minute (16 L per minute) with FiO2 60 percent. Respiratory rate 68, tracheal tug, and marked subcostal recession. Saturations 92 percent, capillary gas pH 7.28 pCO2 62. He is drowsy with poor interaction. Weight is 8 kg. He is otherwise previously well and term.

He was transferred from a smaller peripheral hospital. Retrieval team is 30 minutes away.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 164, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 68 with tracheal tug and recession, SpO2 92% on 60% FiO2, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L (105-135), white cells 12.6 x10^9/L (5-15), CRP 22 mg/L (under 5), capillary pH 7.28 pCO2 62 mmHg lactate 2.6 mmol/L, glucose 4.8 mmol/L
data_table.Imaging: chest X-ray hyperinflation, patchy right upper lobe atelectasis, no consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give IV ceftriaxone 50 mg per kg daily and IV azithromycin 10 mg per kg daily awaiting nasopharyngeal aspirate PCR
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are not indicated in typical viral bronchiolitis without focal consolidation or clear secondary bacterial infection; they do not address respiratory failure. (Source: RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis Guideline)

options.text: Give nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with adrenaline 5 mg back to back and add IV hydrocortisone 4 mg per kg daily
options.rationale: Salbutamol, adrenaline, and steroids are not effective in bronchiolitis and are not recommended; delaying escalation to CPAP with these therapies risks respiratory arrest. (Source: RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis Guideline)

options.text: Escalate to nasal CPAP 7 cmH2O with FiO2 titrated to saturations 92 to 97 percent and consult PICU for retrieval
options.rationale: Severe bronchiolitis with impending failure on HFNC (drowsy, rising CO2, poor perfusion) is escalated to CPAP as the next non-invasive step and PICU is consulted for possible intubation; intubation is reserved for CPAP failure. (Source: RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis Guideline)

options.text: Give 3 percent hypertonic saline nebuliser 4 mL 6 hourly and continue current HFNC settings unchanged
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline has not been shown to improve outcomes in bronchiolitis and does not treat impending respiratory failure; escalation of respiratory support is needed. (Source: RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis Guideline)

options.text: Insert an intercostal chest drain because right upper lobe atelectasis is causing the deterioration on the film
options.rationale: Atelectasis on chest X-ray in bronchiolitis is common and does not require drainage; a chest drain is not indicated without a pneumothorax or significant effusion. (Source: RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis Guideline)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis in infants is treated supportively with oxygen, minimal handling, and feeding support. HFNC is second line after standard oxygen; if the infant tires or CO2 rises, CPAP is next before intubation. Bronchodilators, steroids, adrenaline, hypertonic saline, and antibiotics are not routinely useful. Retrieval to a PICU should be arranged for infants requiring CPAP.
key_points: Escalation ladder: room air, low flow oxygen, HFNC, CPAP, intubation
Bronchodilators and steroids not indicated in bronchiolitis
Antibiotics only if consolidation or clear bacterial coinfection
HFNC typical settings 2 L per kg per minute, capped around 20 L per minute for infants
explanation.pearls: PARIS trial showed HFNC reduces intubation vs standard oxygen in moderate bronchiolitis; escalate to CPAP if HFNC failure, defined as no improvement in RR, HR, work of breathing, or O2 requirement within 1 to 2 hours.

subtopic_detail: Salt-losing crisis in a newborn presenting at day 12
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in ED reviewing a 12 day old baby girl with 3 days of vomiting, poor feeding, and lethargy. She was born at term by vaginal delivery to well parents. Weight is now 2900 g, down from 3200 g at birth. She is dehydrated with sunken fontanelle, cold peripheries, and capillary refill 4 seconds. External genitalia show clitoromegaly with partial labial fusion. The newborn screening result is pending. She is hypotensive at 52/28 with pulse 178. She has not passed urine for 8 hours.

Blood tests return with the values shown.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 178, blood pressure 52/28, respiratory rate 62, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, weight 2900 g
data_table.Bloods: sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 6.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 2.2 mmol/L (2.6-6.0), creatinine 82 umol/L (20-60), bicarbonate 14 mmol/L (22-32), 17-hydroxyprogesterone pending
data_table.Imaging: chest X-ray clear, pelvic ultrasound shows uterus and ovaries present, no testes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give 3 percent hypertonic saline 5 mL per kg IV bolus as first fluid to correct the profound hyponatraemia rapidly
options.rationale: In CAH crisis the hyponatraemia is due to aldosterone deficiency and volume loss, not free water excess; 0.9 percent saline plus hydrocortisone corrects both safely without ODS risk. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

options.text: IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 0.5 mL per kg over 5 minutes and salbutamol nebuliser for the hyperkalaemia first
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia in CAH crisis is driven by cortisol and aldosterone deficiency; giving cortisol, dextrose, and saline addresses the cause and lowers potassium without cardiac protective agents unless there are ECG changes. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

options.text: Start IV dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg 6 hourly as it does not interfere with the diagnostic 17-hydroxyprogesterone
options.rationale: Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and is inappropriate for salt-losing crisis; hydrocortisone provides both glucocorticoid and, at stress dose, mineralocorticoid coverage. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 25 mg bolus, IV 10 percent dextrose 5 mL per kg bolus, and 0.9 percent saline 20 mL per kg bolus
options.rationale: Salt-losing CAH crisis needs immediate parenteral hydrocortisone (bolus then infusion), correction of hypoglycaemia with dextrose 10 percent, and volume expansion with normal saline; potassium falls with these steps and is not initially treated. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

options.text: Withhold steroids until 17-hydroxyprogesterone confirms diagnosis and give only crystalloid resuscitation now
options.rationale: Delaying hydrocortisone in shocked neonate with virilisation and biochemistry consistent with CAH is unsafe; treat empirically after taking cortisol and 17-OHP samples. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

explanation.summary: Salt-losing CAH crisis is treated by immediate IV hydrocortisone (bolus 25 mg then infusion), 10 percent dextrose for hypoglycaemia, and 0.9 percent saline for volume expansion. Blood should be taken for cortisol and 17-hydroxyprogesterone before steroids where possible but treatment should not be delayed. Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and is inappropriate. Hyponatraemia in this setting responds to saline plus hydrocortisone, not hypertonic saline.
key_points: Immediate hydrocortisone (25 mg IV bolus neonate) plus dextrose plus saline
Send cortisol and 17-OHP before steroids where possible but do not delay treatment
Dexamethasone inadequate: no mineralocorticoid activity
Fludrocortisone 100 mcg orally daily added once stable for maintenance
explanation.pearls: Classical 21-hydroxylase deficiency: karyotype 46,XX baby girl with virilised external genitalia, salt-losing crisis in second week of life; stress dose hydrocortisone at 100 mg per m2 per day divided 6 hourly (neonate 25 mg IV bolus then 25 mg 6 hourly).

subtopic_detail: Metaphyseal corner fracture in an 8 month old
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8 month old boy with distress on nappy changes for 2 days. Parents attribute it to constipation. On examination there is bruising of variable ages over the lower back and left thigh, and reluctance to bear weight. X-ray of the left lower limb shows a classic metaphyseal (bucket-handle) fracture of the distal tibia. He is otherwise well nourished. There is no bleeding disorder history and coagulation screen is normal. The family is known socially but has no current welfare involvement.

The consultant asks what steps to take now.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, weight 9.2 kg
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L (105-135), platelets 268 x10^9/L (150-400), INR 1.0, APTT 32 seconds, calcium 2.42 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), alkaline phosphatase 220 U/L (110-320)
data_table.Imaging: left distal tibia classic metaphyseal fracture, bruising photographed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Splint the fracture and refer to community fracture clinic in 1 week without hospital admission or notification
options.rationale: Discharging a pre-mobile infant with a highly specific abuse fracture back to an unassessed environment risks further serious harm; admission and notification are mandatory. (Source: RCH Melbourne Child Abuse Guideline)

options.text: Reassure parents that these bucket-handle fractures are common accidental injuries and discharge with GP follow up
options.rationale: Classic metaphyseal lesions are highly specific for non-accidental injury in a pre-mobile child and warrant safeguarding assessment; discharge without further work up would fail the child. (Source: RCH Melbourne Child Abuse Guideline)

options.text: Discuss confidentially with mother alone before notifying anyone, to preserve therapeutic relationship first
options.rationale: Mandatory reporting overrides confidentiality when there is reasonable suspicion of child abuse; discussion should be professional and honest but must not delay notification to child protection services. (Source: RCH Melbourne Child Abuse Guideline)

options.text: Order metabolic bone disease workup and delay child protection notification until osteogenesis imperfecta is excluded
options.rationale: Metabolic workup can be done in parallel but does not delay notification; osteogenesis imperfecta does not typically cause classic metaphyseal fractures, and safeguarding takes priority. (Source: RCH Melbourne Child Abuse Guideline)

options.text: Admit for child protection assessment, notify the state child protection service, and arrange full skeletal survey and ophthalmology review
options.rationale: A classic metaphyseal fracture in an infant is highly specific for inflicted injury; admission, mandatory notification, skeletal survey per RANZCR protocol, and ophthalmology examination for retinal haemorrhages are standard. (Source: RCH Melbourne Child Abuse Guideline)

explanation.summary: Classic metaphyseal lesions (bucket-handle or corner fractures) in infants are highly specific for inflicted trauma. Management includes admission, mandatory notification to child protection services, full skeletal survey per RANZCR paediatric imaging protocol, ophthalmology examination for retinal haemorrhages, and MDT involvement including social work. Confidentiality is overridden by mandatory reporting duties.
key_points: Classic metaphyseal fracture in an infant is highly specific for NAI
Mandatory notification to child protection: does not require consent
Full skeletal survey per RANZCR paediatric imaging protocol, repeat at 11 to 14 days
Fundoscopy for retinal haemorrhages, consider neuroimaging under 2 years
explanation.pearls: RANZCR paediatric skeletal survey includes AP and lateral skull, chest, abdomen, spine, humeri, forearms, hands, femora, tibiae, and feet; repeat limited survey 11 to 14 days later increases yield by up to 25 percent as callus becomes visible.

subtopic_detail: Hypoxia and new infiltrate in a child with HbSS
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 11 year old boy with known homozygous sickle cell disease admitted with a vaso-occlusive crisis 2 days ago. Overnight he has developed pleuritic chest pain, temperature 38.6, oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, and a new right sided infiltrate on chest X-ray. He is on morphine PCA. Baseline haemoglobin is 82 with 20 percent HbF. Current Hb is 68 with reticulocytes 15 percent. He has never had an exchange transfusion.

The haematology consultant has reviewed the case with the intensivist by phone.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 108/68, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 89% on room air rising to 94% on 8 L Hudson, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 68 g/L (baseline 82), reticulocytes 15%, platelets 486 x10^9/L, LDH 1240 U/L (140-280), bilirubin 62 umol/L (0-20), CRP 88 mg/L (under 5)
data_table.Imaging: chest X-ray new right lower lobe infiltrate, cardiomegaly borderline, no effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin, IV fluids at maintenance, oxygen therapy, and urgent exchange transfusion
options.rationale: Acute chest syndrome with hypoxia and dropping haemoglobin needs broad antibiotics for atypicals and encapsulated organisms, careful fluid balance, oxygen, and exchange transfusion to lower HbS below 30 percent. Simple top-up transfusion is used only in mild cases. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Acute Guidelines)

options.text: IV fluids at 1.5 times maintenance, oral amoxicillin only, continue morphine PCA, and no transfusion needed today
options.rationale: Over-hydration precipitates pulmonary oedema in ACS, oral amoxicillin does not cover atypicals, and hypoxia with falling haemoglobin needs transfusion. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Acute Guidelines)

options.text: Give hydroxycarbamide 20 mg per kg orally daily today and stop opioids to reduce respiratory depression risk
options.rationale: Hydroxycarbamide is chronic prophylaxis and does not treat acute chest syndrome; stopping opioids leads to inadequate analgesia and shallow breathing worsening atelectasis. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Acute Guidelines)

options.text: Give a simple top-up transfusion 20 mL per kg only and continue amoxicillin monotherapy without exchange
options.rationale: Simple top-up alone in severe ACS with hypoxia and multilobar or clinical deterioration is insufficient; exchange transfusion targeting HbS under 30 percent is preferred in severe disease. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Acute Guidelines)

options.text: Nebulised bronchodilators and IV hydrocortisone as first line therapy without antibiotics until sputum returns
options.rationale: Bronchodilators and steroids are not standard for ACS; delaying antibiotics in a febrile hypoxic child with sickle disease risks progression to sepsis and death. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Acute Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute chest syndrome is diagnosed by a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest X-ray plus one of fever, respiratory symptoms, or hypoxia in a patient with sickle cell disease. Management is oxygen, judicious IV fluid, IV antibiotics (cephalosporin plus macrolide), effective analgesia and incentive spirometry to prevent atelectasis, and transfusion. Exchange transfusion is preferred when hypoxia is severe, multilobar, or deteriorating; simple top-up is used for milder cases.
key_points: ACS: new infiltrate plus fever, respiratory symptoms, or hypoxia in SCD
IV cephalosporin plus macrolide, oxygen, incentive spirometry, adequate analgesia
Exchange transfusion for severe ACS (SpO2 under 90, multilobar, deteriorating)
Simple top-up transfusion for milder ACS with Hb below baseline
explanation.pearls: BSH target HbS below 30 percent post exchange, keep total Hb 100 to 110 g/L to avoid hyperviscosity; incentive spirometry every 2 hours reduces ACS progression in vaso-occlusive crises by around 50 percent.

subtopic_detail: IVIG-resistant disease with giant coronary aneurysm at echo
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3 year old boy with Kawasaki disease, day 10 of illness. He received IVIG 2 g per kg 48 hours ago and remains febrile at 39 degrees with persistent conjunctivitis, rash, and irritability. Echocardiography today shows a giant right coronary artery aneurysm 8 mm in diameter (Z score plus 12) with intraluminal thrombus signal. Platelets have risen to 820. He is on aspirin 3 mg per kg daily. He has no allergy. Renal and liver function are normal.

The paediatric cardiologist has been consulted by phone.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 152, blood pressure 96/62, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.0 degrees Celsius, weight 15 kg
data_table.Bloods: Hb 108 g/L (110-140), platelets 820 x10^9/L (150-400), white cells 15.4 x10^9/L (5-15), CRP 128 mg/L (under 5), ferritin 480 ng/mL (7-140)
data_table.Imaging: echocardiogram giant right coronary aneurysm 8 mm Z score +12 with thrombus, LV function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue aspirin monotherapy at antiplatelet dose and repeat echocardiography in 2 weeks without other change
options.rationale: Aspirin monotherapy is inadequate for IVIG-resistant KD with giant aneurysm and thrombus; ongoing inflammation and thrombus need dual escalation. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Statement 2017)

options.text: Give a second dose IVIG 2 g per kg plus IV methylprednisolone 30 mg per kg daily for 3 days, add therapeutic enoxaparin
options.rationale: IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease with giant coronary aneurysm and intraluminal thrombus needs second dose IVIG plus corticosteroids for inflammation control, plus therapeutic anticoagulation for thrombus prevention or treatment. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Statement 2017)

options.text: Stop aspirin because of the platelet count over 800 and start apixaban 2.5 mg orally twice daily as monotherapy
options.rationale: Aspirin is continued in KD for antiplatelet effect on coronary arteries regardless of platelet count; DOACs are not first line in paediatric KD anticoagulation. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Statement 2017)

options.text: Give infliximab 5 mg per kg IV single dose alone without repeat IVIG or corticosteroids and no anticoagulation added
options.rationale: Infliximab is a second line option after IVIG plus steroids fail; giving it alone without repeat IVIG or steroids and without anticoagulation for the thrombus is inadequate. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Statement 2017)

options.text: Refer for coronary artery bypass grafting now because of giant aneurysm and thrombus formation on echo
options.rationale: CABG is reserved for coronary ischaemia or severe stenosis, not first line for giant aneurysm with fresh thrombus in a febrile child; medical intensification with IVIG, steroids, and anticoagulation is standard. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Statement 2017)

explanation.summary: IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease is treated with a second IVIG dose plus adjunctive corticosteroids (either short pulses of IV methylprednisolone or oral prednisolone taper). Refractory cases can escalate to infliximab or ciclosporin. Giant coronary aneurysms (Z score over 10 or luminal diameter over 8 mm) require therapeutic anticoagulation with warfarin or LMWH plus aspirin, and long term follow up with cardiology.
key_points: IVIG resistance: retreat with IVIG 2 g per kg plus corticosteroids
Third line escalation: infliximab or ciclosporin
Giant aneurysm (Z over 10 or over 8 mm): dual therapy aspirin plus LMWH or warfarin
Coronary events managed medically first, surgery reserved for ischaemia
explanation.pearls: RAISE trial showed adding IV methylprednisolone 2 mg per kg per day to IVIG reduced coronary abnormalities in high risk Japanese cohort; Kobayashi score is validated in Japanese but has lower sensitivity in Western cohorts, so clinical judgement dominates in Australia.

subtopic_detail: Peanut aspiration with unilateral wheeze in a toddler
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in ED reviewing a 2 year old girl brought in 4 hours after a witnessed choking episode while eating peanuts. She had brief coughing and stridor at the time that settled. On examination she now has right sided monophonic wheeze, reduced air entry on the right, and no cyanosis. Saturations are 96 percent on room air. Chest X-ray shows subtle hyperinflation of the right lung on expiratory film with mediastinal shift to the left. She is stable and playing in the cubicle.

A tertiary paediatric ENT team is available.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, weight 12 kg
data_table.Imaging: chest X-ray inspiratory film unremarkable, expiratory film shows right lung hyperinflation with mediastinal shift left, no consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Physiotherapy with back slaps and postural drainage on the paediatric ward as first line intervention
options.rationale: Blind physiotherapy manoeuvres can dislodge the foreign body into the trachea causing complete airway obstruction; bronchoscopy is definitive management for suspected lodged aspiration. (Source: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline)
source_refs: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg and oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg then discharge with 24 hour open access review
options.rationale: Bronchodilators do not remove a foreign body; discharging a child with likely retained peanut risks pneumonia, post obstructive collapse, and migration. (Source: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline)
source_refs: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline

options.text: Arrange urgent transfer for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthetic by paediatric ENT to extract the foreign body
options.rationale: Witnessed choking episode with peanut and persistent unilateral wheeze plus expiratory air trapping is highly suggestive of a lodged organic foreign body; rigid bronchoscopy under GA is the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic procedure. (Source: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline)
source_refs: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline

options.text: Give oral antibiotics amoxicillin 25 mg per kg 8 hourly for 5 days and repeat chest X-ray in 48 hours
options.rationale: Antibiotics without removal do not treat the mechanical cause of air trapping and delay bronchoscopic extraction, increasing complication risk. (Source: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline)
source_refs: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline

options.text: Order CT chest to confirm the foreign body location before deciding whether bronchoscopy is required
options.rationale: CT is not required before bronchoscopy when history and expiratory hyperinflation strongly suggest aspiration; it adds radiation, delay, and may not visualise organic material well. (Source: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline)
source_refs: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline

explanation.summary: Witnessed choking on nut or organic material followed by persistent unilateral wheeze, reduced air entry, or expiratory air trapping is a strong indication for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthetic. Imaging cannot exclude foreign body aspiration, and delaying bronchoscopy risks post obstructive pneumonia and mucosal damage. Blind physiotherapy manoeuvres are unsafe.
key_points: Witnessed choking plus focal signs: rigid bronchoscopy under GA
Expiratory chest X-ray or fluoroscopy shows air trapping on affected side
Normal imaging does not exclude aspiration
Avoid blind back slaps, chest physiotherapy, or upright posturing
explanation.pearls: Peanut is the most commonly aspirated organic foreign body under 3 years; right main bronchus is more commonly involved due to more vertical anatomy; ventilation lung scan can localise atypical cases if X-ray is normal.

sources.label: RCH Melbourne Foreign Body Aspiration Guideline

subtopic_detail: Impending obstruction with stridor at rest and marked recession
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in ED reviewing an 18 month old boy with 2 days of barking cough now with continuous stridor at rest, marked sternal recession, agitation, and mottled peripheries. Saturations are 91 percent on 4 L Hudson mask. Weight is 12 kg. Temperature is 38.2. He has not received prior steroids. He is drooling minimally with no fever until this morning, and had been fully immunised. No foreign body history reported by parents.

The anaesthetist and ENT team are aware and coming to the department.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 178, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 56 with marked recession, SpO2 91% on 4 L Hudson, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius, GCS 14 agitated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg back to back and oral ibuprofen and paracetamol for fever without steroid therapy
options.rationale: Salbutamol has no role in croup because obstruction is subglottic oedema, not bronchospasm; steroids are the cornerstone therapy. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

options.text: IV cefotaxime 50 mg per kg 8 hourly empirically and lateral neck X-ray urgently to exclude epiglottitis
options.rationale: Barking cough with viral prodrome is classic croup, not epiglottitis; distressing the child for X-ray in impending obstruction can precipitate complete airway loss. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg alone and observe on the ward for 4 hours before reassessment for adrenaline
options.rationale: Severe croup with stridor at rest needs nebulised adrenaline immediately for airway oedema; oral prednisolone alone acts too slowly and observation risks obstruction. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 1 in 1000 5 mL, oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kg, minimise handling, and prepare for possible intubation
options.rationale: Severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession is treated with nebulised adrenaline for immediate airway oedema relief, corticosteroids (dexamethasone) for sustained benefit, minimal handling to avoid distress, and anaesthetic and ENT standby for intubation if needed. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

options.text: Insert IV line and give bolus IV hydrocortisone 4 mg per kg and 20 mL per kg saline before any nebulised treatment
options.rationale: Distressing the child with IV access in impending obstruction can precipitate airway loss; oral or IM dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline are preferred first steps. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe croup with stridor at rest, marked recession, or hypoxia is treated with nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone. Minimise handling to avoid worsening obstruction. Anaesthetic and ENT standby is essential in impending failure. Bronchodilators have no role and epiglottitis is rare in immunised children. IV access in a distressed child should be delayed until the airway is secured or improving.
key_points: Severe croup: nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 solution
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kg oral (max 12 mg) or IM if unable to swallow
Minimise handling, no unnecessary investigations, ENT plus anaesthetics standby
Salbutamol and antibiotics not indicated in typical viral croup
explanation.pearls: RCH Melbourne uses dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kg oral (up to 12 mg) as first line; prednisolone 1 mg per kg per day for 3 days is an alternative but with slightly higher relapse rate; observation for at least 3 to 4 hours after adrenaline to detect rebound.

subtopic_detail: IVIG timing decision on day 5 of fever
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3 year old girl on day 5 of fever above 39 degrees Celsius unresponsive to paracetamol and ibuprofen. She has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, a strawberry tongue with cracked lips, an erythematous polymorphous truncal rash, and unilateral right cervical lymphadenopathy 1.6 cm across. Her hands and feet are swollen and tender. Coronary artery Z-scores are within normal limits on echocardiogram. She has had no other viral prodrome and no exposure to measles cases. Weight 14 kg.

Investigations show a raised CRP and platelet count with sterile pyuria.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: haemoglobin 102 g/L (110-140), white cell count 17.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), neutrophils 12.9 x10^9/L (1.5-8.5), platelets 462 x10^9/L (150-450), CRP 138 mg/L (<5), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), ALT 68 U/L (<40)
data_table.Urine: sterile pyuria, no bacteria, no nitrites
data_table.Echocardiogram: coronary Z-scores within normal limits, no aneurysm, normal LV function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment now?

options.text: Await culture and CRP trend for 48 hours before starting immunomodulatory therapy for this child
options.rationale: Delayed IVIG beyond day 10 substantially increases coronary aneurysm risk; complete clinical criteria on day 5 with raised inflammatory markers meet treatment threshold without further delay. (Source: RCH Melbourne Kawasaki Disease Guideline)

options.text: IV methylprednisolone 30 mg per kg pulse followed by oral prednisolone taper as sole primary therapy
options.rationale: Steroid monotherapy is reserved for high-risk features (Kobayashi score) as adjunct to IVIG or for IVIG-resistant disease; it is not first-line alone. (Source: RCH Melbourne Kawasaki Disease Guideline)

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 50 mg per kg with a lumbar puncture to exclude bacterial infection prior to further therapy
options.rationale: Sterile pyuria and prolonged fever are classic Kawasaki features and not indications for empirical antibiotics; LP is not required and would delay definitive therapy. (Source: RCH Melbourne Kawasaki Disease Guideline)

options.text: IV immunoglobulin 2 g per kg single infusion over 10 hours with high-dose aspirin 30 mg per kg per day
options.rationale: Complete criteria (fever plus at least 4 of 5 principal features) on day 5 with raised CRP indicates prompt IVIG 2 g/kg with high-dose aspirin (30-50 mg/kg/day divided) until afebrile 48 hours, then low-dose aspirin. (Source: RCH Melbourne Kawasaki Disease Guideline)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 2 mg per kg per day with a repeat echocardiogram scheduled at 2 weeks for progression
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone alone is not first-line; delaying IVIG allows continued vasculitis and increases coronary aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH Melbourne Kawasaki Disease Guideline)

explanation.summary: Complete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed on fever of 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 principal features (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, mucous membrane changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy). IVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin within the first 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm risk from around 25 percent to under 5 percent. Sterile pyuria, transaminitis, and hyponatraemia support the diagnosis. Coronary artery involvement can develop after initial normal echocardiography, so treatment is not withheld while awaiting imaging change.
key_points: IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 hours plus aspirin 30-50 mg/kg/day divided
Treat within 10 days of fever onset; earlier is better
Normal initial echo does not exclude Kawasaki nor delay IVIG
Sterile pyuria supports Kawasaki, not UTI
explanation.pearls: Kobayashi score >=5 flags IVIG-resistance risk and prompts adjunctive IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg with the first IVIG dose; refractory fever 36 hours after IVIG triggers second-dose IVIG plus consideration of infliximab.

subtopic_detail: Adrenaline dose with biphasic risk features
stem:
You are the intern in a rural emergency department when a 4 year old boy is carried in by his mother 20 minutes after eating a peanut butter sandwich. He has generalised urticaria, marked lip and tongue swelling, audible wheeze, and vomiting. He weighs an estimated 18 kg. He received oral loratadine at home with no benefit. He has previously had a mild peanut reaction only. The nearest tertiary paediatric centre is 90 minutes by road.

His mother has an adult EpiPen in her bag which has not yet been given.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 160, blood pressure 78/40, respiratory rate 40 with subcostal recession, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: widespread urticaria, tongue swelling, expiratory wheeze bilaterally, prolonged capillary refill 3 seconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intramuscular adrenaline treatment?

options.text: IM adrenaline 180 micrograms calculated as 10 micrograms per kg into the lateral thigh with reassessment
options.rationale: ASCIA uses banded IM adrenaline doses to avoid arithmetic under pressure; 10 mcg/kg calculation is IV emergency dosing and is not first-line IM in a child collapsed at the roadside. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: IM adrenaline 150 micrograms into the deltoid muscle with a second dose planned only if progression continues
options.rationale: EpiPen Jr 150 mcg is for 10-20 kg per ASCIA but the child is 18 kg with hypotension; the adult 300 mcg dose is preferred at borderline weight with shock, and anterolateral thigh is preferred over deltoid. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: IM adrenaline 300 micrograms into the anterolateral thigh with repeat every 5 minutes if response is inadequate
options.rationale: ASCIA-banded IM adrenaline for 20 kg or under 6 years is 300 mcg (EpiPen dose); anterolateral thigh gives fastest absorption and can be repeated every 5 min while preparing IV access. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mg with high flow oxygen while an IV is inserted for the first adrenaline dose
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is adjunct for upper airway oedema (croup or laryngeal angioedema); it does not treat shock or systemic anaphylaxis and delaying IM adrenaline while gaining IV access is unsafe. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: IV adrenaline 10 micrograms per kg bolus after establishing intravenous access as the first-line management step
options.rationale: IV adrenaline boluses are for arrest or refractory shock only and carry arrhythmia risk; delaying immediate IM adrenaline to gain IV access in a child with progressing airway swelling is unsafe. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis with hypotension, airway oedema, and respiratory compromise is a time-critical intervention. IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh at ASCIA banded doses (150 mcg for 10-20 kg, 300 mcg for over 20 kg) is first-line and can be repeated every 5 minutes. Do not delay the first IM dose to gain IV access. IV adrenaline infusion is reserved for refractory shock in a monitored setting.
key_points: ASCIA banded IM adrenaline: 150 mcg (10-20 kg), 300 mcg (>20 kg)
Anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 min if inadequate response
Give supine with legs elevated unless respiratory distress precludes
Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts, not primary treatment
explanation.pearls: Biphasic reactions occur in around 5 percent of paediatric anaphylaxis, usually within 4-8 hours; ASCIA advises minimum 4 hours observation after last dose, longer if repeated adrenaline was needed or severe features present.

subtopic_detail: Bilirubin threshold with G6PD risk factor
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the postnatal ward. A 62 hour old term male born by uncomplicated vaginal birth is referred by the midwife for visible jaundice extending to the abdomen. Birth weight 3.4 kg, current weight 3.15 kg. The mother is exclusively breastfeeding with reported difficulty at latch; the baby has had 4 wet nappies today. Parents originate from South East Asia. Blood group B positive; mother is O positive. Direct antiglobulin test is negative.

The midwife is concerned about family history of a first-degree cousin needing exchange transfusion as a neonate.

data_table.Vital signs: temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, heart rate 148, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Bloods: total serum bilirubin 310 micromol/L, conjugated 8 micromol/L, haemoglobin 168 g/L (150-200 neonate), reticulocytes 4.2 percent, blood film not yet reviewed
data_table.Feeding: exclusive breastfeeding, 7 percent weight loss from birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence single conventional phototherapy and reassess bilirubin in 4 to 6 hours before further therapy
options.rationale: At 62 hours and 310 micromol/L with a G6PD deficiency risk factor (Asian ethnicity, family history of exchange), the threshold shifts down and intensive phototherapy is warranted rather than single-bank conventional. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

options.text: Commence intensive multiple phototherapy with hydration support and request urgent G6PD screening now
options.rationale: Bilirubin 310 micromol/L at 62 hours with the family history and Asian heritage places this baby above the phototherapy threshold using the RCH lowered risk-factor line; intensive phototherapy with hydration and urgent G6PD assay is indicated. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

options.text: Arrange exchange transfusion urgently as the bilirubin will otherwise reach kernicterus threshold within hours
options.rationale: Exchange thresholds at 62 hours are well above 310 micromol/L on RCH charts even with risk factors; intensive phototherapy is first-line and typically averts exchange when started promptly. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

options.text: Change to formula feeding for 24 hours as breast milk jaundice is the most likely explanation now
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice presents later (day 7 onward) and interrupting breastfeeding is not first-line; the current picture is early with a risk factor requiring phototherapy while supporting continued breastfeeding. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

options.text: Continue breastfeeding without phototherapy and repeat serum bilirubin in 12 hours as the trend is reassuring
options.rationale: The absolute value with risk factors already exceeds the intervention threshold; deferring 12 hours risks bilirubin rising into exchange range and preventable neurotoxicity. (Source: RCH Melbourne Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Neonatal phototherapy thresholds are age (in hours) and risk-factor dependent. RCH Melbourne charts use a lower risk-factor line for babies with haemolysis (positive DAT or G6PD deficiency), sepsis, prematurity, temperature instability, or low albumin. Family history and Asian heritage support G6PD screening. Intensive multiple phototherapy with adequate hydration should start once the threshold is crossed, with reassessment at 4-6 hours. Continued breastfeeding is supported alongside phototherapy.
key_points: Use age-in-hours charts; do not rely on absolute number alone
Risk factors shift threshold down: G6PD, sepsis, prematurity, DAT+
Intensive phototherapy: multiple banks, maximise skin exposure
Continue breastfeeding; supplement only if weight loss >10 percent
explanation.pearls: G6PD deficiency is X-linked and affects up to 10-15 percent of males in Mediterranean, Southeast Asian, and African populations; oxidative haemolysis can occur without an obvious trigger in neonates because of transient enzyme deficiency in RBC precursors.

subtopic_detail: Atypical presentation with a normal ultrasound and ongoing pain
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9 month old boy brought in with 12 hours of intermittent inconsolable crying with his legs drawn up, in between which he is quiet and drowsy. The mother reports one loose stool with a small amount of red material she thought looked like jelly. He has vomited twice with no green content. He is fully immunised. Bedside abdominal ultrasound performed 2 hours ago by the paediatric radiology fellow showed no target sign but did not fully visualise the right upper quadrant due to bowel gas.

He has become quieter over the last 40 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 152, blood pressure 88/54, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: abdomen soft with vague right sided fullness, no peritonism, bowel sounds normal
data_table.Bloods: haemoglobin 108 g/L (105-135), venous lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2), CRP 12 mg/L (<5)
data_table.Prior imaging: ultrasound 2 hours ago inconclusive with poor right upper quadrant view

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol and safety-net advice as an inconclusive ultrasound rules out intussusception
options.rationale: An inconclusive ultrasound (technically limited view) does not exclude intussusception; classic triad plus rising lactate and worsening drowsiness demands repeat imaging or definitive management, not discharge. (Source: RCH Melbourne Intussusception Guideline)

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound urgently with a paediatric radiologist and prepare surgical team for immediate operative intervention
options.rationale: Repeat ultrasound is reasonable but skipping to immediate operative intervention before confirming a diagnosis or attempting radiological reduction is not the standard pathway when the child has no peritonism. (Source: RCH Melbourne Intussusception Guideline)

options.text: Perform an abdominal X-ray series in supine and erect views as the primary imaging modality for further assessment
options.rationale: Plain films have low sensitivity for intussusception and are used to look for perforation, not to make the diagnosis; ultrasound by an experienced operator is the modality of choice. (Source: RCH Melbourne Intussusception Guideline)

options.text: Give IV ceftriaxone 50 mg per kg for suspected sepsis and admit for observation with 4 hourly abdominal examinations
options.rationale: Sepsis alone does not fit the intermittent colic with drawing up of legs pattern; treating for sepsis without repeating imaging risks a missed surgical diagnosis and infarcted bowel. (Source: RCH Melbourne Intussusception Guideline)

options.text: Arrange repeat ultrasound now with the paediatric radiologist and prepare for possible air enema after resuscitation
options.rationale: Classic triad, worsening drowsiness, elevated lactate, and inconclusive first scan warrant repeat imaging with an experienced operator; if intussusception confirmed and no peritonism or perforation, air enema reduction after IV fluids and NG decompression is first-line. (Source: RCH Melbourne Intussusception Guideline)

explanation.summary: Intussusception in a child 3 months to 3 years old classically presents with intermittent colicky pain (legs drawn up), quiet interictal periods, vomiting and later red material stools. Ultrasound sensitivity approaches 98 percent in expert hands but a technically limited scan does not exclude the diagnosis. Rising lactate, tachycardia, and drowsiness suggest bowel compromise. Confirm with repeat expert ultrasound and manage with fluid resuscitation, NG decompression, and air enema reduction; laparotomy is reserved for perforation, peritonism, or failed reduction.
key_points: Classic triad: colic, red material stool, sausage-shaped mass
Ultrasound is first-line; a limited scan is not exclusion
Air enema reduction after resuscitation is definitive when no peritonism
Laparotomy for peritonism, perforation, or failed radiological reduction
explanation.pearls: Enema reduction has 85-90 percent success in typical ileocolic intussusception under 48 hours; recurrence rate is around 10 percent, higher after operative reduction than after air enema.

subtopic_detail: Late presentation with cardiovascular workup priority
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 13 year old girl referred by the general practitioner for delayed puberty. She has had no thelarche and no menarche. Her height is 141 cm (below the third centile) and her mid-parental target is 165 cm. She has a webbed neck, cubitus valgus, and short fourth metacarpals. Blood pressure in the right arm is 148/92; in the leg 118/76. She has had recurrent otitis media in childhood and now uses hearing aids intermittently. Screening bloods show FSH markedly raised and oestradiol undetectable.

Her mother asks what investigation is most urgent to arrange first.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 84, right arm blood pressure 148/92, right leg blood pressure 118/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99%
data_table.Bloods: FSH 68 IU/L (age-adjusted <10 pre-pubertal), LH 22 IU/L, oestradiol undetectable, thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Growth: height 141 cm below 3rd centile, weight 40 kg 10th centile
data_table.Examination: webbed neck, low posterior hairline, cubitus valgus, no goitre

lead_in: Which investigation is the highest priority next?

options.text: Karyotype analysis with reflex fluorescence in situ hybridisation for Y chromosome material to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Karyotype is essential and should be sent, but the clinical picture is already highly suggestive and immediate priority is characterising the cardiovascular lesion causing radiofemoral BP delay before initiating any therapy. (Source: Turner Syndrome Clinical Practice Guidelines 2017)

options.text: Bone age radiograph of the left wrist and hand for skeletal maturity assessment before commencing growth hormone
options.rationale: Bone age informs growth hormone timing but is not the most urgent step; missing a coarctation risks aortic dissection, and cardiac assessment must precede endocrine therapy planning. (Source: Turner Syndrome Clinical Practice Guidelines 2017)

options.text: Pelvic ultrasound to assess uterine size and ovarian remnants prior to hormone replacement discussions with the family
options.rationale: Pelvic ultrasound informs later fertility counselling and oestrogen induction planning but is not the most urgent investigation given the radiofemoral BP gradient requiring immediate cardiovascular workup. (Source: Turner Syndrome Clinical Practice Guidelines 2017)

options.text: Transthoracic echocardiogram with cardiac MRI referral for suspected coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve assessment
options.rationale: Radiofemoral gradient with upper limb hypertension in a phenotypic Turner girl strongly suggests coarctation, present in around 10 percent; bicuspid aortic valve in around 30 percent; TTE plus cardiac MRI is priority to guide urgent intervention and pre-empt aortic dissection risk. (Source: Turner Syndrome Clinical Practice Guidelines 2017)

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound to look for horseshoe kidney or duplex system as one component of the multisystem screen
options.rationale: Renal ultrasound is part of the Turner screening panel (30 to 40 percent have anomalies) but is not more urgent than characterising a suspected coarctation causing measurable BP gradient. (Source: Turner Syndrome Clinical Practice Guidelines 2017)

explanation.summary: Turner syndrome (45,X and mosaic variants) commonly presents with short stature, delayed puberty, and characteristic dysmorphology. A radiofemoral BP gradient and upper limb hypertension flag coarctation of the aorta, present in around 10 percent, alongside bicuspid aortic valve in around 30 percent. Cardiac MRI complements echocardiography to define aortic arch anatomy and dilation risk. Karyotype confirms the diagnosis but should not delay urgent cardiovascular characterisation. Growth hormone, oestrogen induction, and multisystem screening follow.
key_points: Coarctation, bicuspid AV, aortic dilation drive early cardiac priority
TTE plus cardiac MRI (or CT if MRI contraindicated)
Karyotype confirms diagnosis; do not delay imaging
Multisystem screen: renal ultrasound, hearing, thyroid, glucose
explanation.pearls: Aortic dissection lifetime risk in Turner syndrome is around 1 to 2 percent, disproportionately in those with hypertension, bicuspid valve, or coarctation; annual cardiac imaging surveillance is recommended from diagnosis.

subtopic_detail: Vague symptoms with normal shunt series but raised ICP suspicion
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6 year old boy with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt inserted for post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus at 3 months. He presents with 3 days of intermittent morning headache with vomiting, unsteady gait for 24 hours, and one episode of double vision this morning. He is afebrile, alert, and cooperative on examination. Neurosurgery reviewed him yesterday and shunt series X-rays and non-contrast CT head showed no discontinuity, no migration, and ventricular sizes similar to baseline scan 2 years ago. Fundoscopy today shows blurred disc margins.

He has become quieter in the last hour and complains of blurred vision now.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 132/82, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: cranial nerves normal apart from bilateral papilloedema, gait wide-based, no focal weakness
data_table.Prior imaging: shunt series unremarkable, non-contrast CT ventricles unchanged from baseline
data_table.Family: mother reports similar pattern preceded shunt revision at 4 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure and discharge with paediatric follow-up in one week as imaging and shunt series are normal today
options.rationale: Papilloedema, morning vomiting, ataxia and diplopia with the mother's previous shunt-failure pattern are classic raised ICP even with unchanged imaging; discharge risks decompensation and death. (Source: RCH Melbourne VP Shunt Guideline)

options.text: Contact neurosurgery for urgent shunt tap and MRI as clinical features suggest malfunction despite unchanged CT
options.rationale: Imaging can appear unchanged in slit-ventricle physiology or partial obstruction; the syndrome (papilloedema, ataxia, diplopia, mother's pattern recognition) mandates neurosurgical shunt tap for ICP measurement and MRI to reassess, not repeat plain imaging alone. (Source: RCH Melbourne VP Shunt Guideline)

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement to distinguish shunt malfunction from idiopathic hypertension
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture in suspected obstructive shunt malfunction risks tonsillar herniation because CSF flow around the outflow obstruction may be compromised; it is contraindicated as a first step. (Source: RCH Melbourne VP Shunt Guideline)

options.text: Give IV mannitol 0.5 g per kg empirically and admit for neurological observations for the next 24 hours
options.rationale: Mannitol without a plan for definitive shunt evaluation delays diagnosis; the priority is neurosurgical assessment with shunt tap and MRI, and empirical osmotic therapy is reserved for herniation signs. (Source: RCH Melbourne VP Shunt Guideline)

options.text: Request repeat non-contrast CT head in 4 hours and consult general paediatrics for admission and observation on the ward
options.rationale: Repeating CT without neurosurgical shunt evaluation misses functional obstruction with minimal ventricular change (slit-ventricle syndrome); MRI plus shunt tap by neurosurgery is required. (Source: RCH Melbourne VP Shunt Guideline)

explanation.summary: Shunt malfunction in a chronic shunt patient must be diagnosed clinically, not by imaging alone. Slit-ventricle physiology and partial obstruction can produce raised ICP with unchanged CT ventricular size. Morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema, sixth nerve palsy, ataxia, and parental pattern-recognition are the syndrome. MRI (with or without shunt-flow sequences) and neurosurgical shunt tap measure function directly. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated because tonsillar herniation risk is high with outflow obstruction.
key_points: Diagnose shunt malfunction clinically, not by CT alone
Slit-ventricle syndrome has minimal ventricular change
Neurosurgical shunt tap and MRI are diagnostic
Avoid LP in obstructive shunt failure
explanation.pearls: Around 40 percent of paediatric shunts fail within 2 years and 50 percent within 5 years; median shunt survival is 6 years, with obstruction the commonest cause followed by infection and disconnection.

subtopic_detail: Late presentation with atypical timing and dehydration in a virilised infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional emergency department. A 24 day old infant labelled female at birth is brought in by parents with 3 days of poor feeding and 12 hours of persistent vomiting. Birth was at 39 weeks by uncomplicated caesarean; newborn screen results are pending. Parents describe an unusually enlarged clitoris that was noted by the midwife but attributed to birth trauma. Weight is 3.0 kg (birth 3.4 kg). The infant is drowsy with a sunken fontanelle. Bedside gas shows metabolic acidosis with hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia. Blood glucose is low.

Your ED has no paediatric endocrinology cover; the tertiary team is on the phone.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 178, blood pressure 62/38, respiratory rate 54, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, apparently enlarged clitoris with partially fused labia, hyperpigmented genitalia
data_table.Bloods: sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 2.1 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), venous pH 7.14, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22-32)
data_table.Access: peripheral IV secured, no central access

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give IV normal saline 20 mL per kg bolus with IV dextrose 2 mL per kg of 10 percent and IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat
options.rationale: Salt-losing CAH crisis needs volume with 0.9 percent saline (avoid hypotonic), IV glucose for hypoglycaemia, and IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat for the infant regardless of exact dose calculation while endocrine advice is sought; this is the RCH salt-losing crisis pathway. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

options.text: Give IV 4 percent dextrose in quarter saline 20 mL per kg with fludrocortisone 100 micrograms orally and calcium gluconate for hyperkalaemia
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid worsens the hyponatraemia; oral fludrocortisone is too slow and unreliable in a vomiting infant; IV hydrocortisone provides the acute glucocorticoid plus mineralocorticoid activity needed at stress dose. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

options.text: Correct hyponatraemia with 3 percent saline 3 mL per kg over 10 minutes as the immediate priority before other therapy
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures or severe symptomatic hyponatraemia; in salt-losing crisis, volume replacement with 0.9 percent saline plus hydrocortisone corrects sodium physiologically without rapid rise and osmotic demyelination risk. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

options.text: Give IV insulin 0.1 units per kg with 50 percent dextrose 1 mL per kg to shift potassium before adrenal steroid therapy
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose shift risks worsening the already-low glucose; hyperkalaemia in salt-losing CAH corrects with volume replacement plus hydrocortisone acting on the aldosterone-deficient state; insulin shift is a distraction and dangerous here. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

options.text: Await 17-hydroxyprogesterone result and the endocrinology team consult before giving any steroid therapy or bolus fluids
options.rationale: Waiting for 17-OHP results before treating a shocked hypoglycaemic infant with virilisation and salt-wasting picture would risk arrest; treat empirically and confirm biochemistry after resuscitation samples are drawn. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

explanation.summary: Salt-losing congenital adrenal hyperplasia (usually 21-hydroxylase deficiency) classically presents around 1-3 weeks of life with vomiting, poor feeding, dehydration, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and hypoglycaemia. Virilised external genitalia in a 46,XX infant may be missed or attributed to birth trauma. Newborn screening detects most but results are not always available at presentation. Immediate treatment is 0.9 percent saline for volume, IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia, and stress-dose IV hydrocortisone (25 mg in infants; 50 mg in children; 100 mg in adolescents) before biochemistry confirmation. Take pre-treatment blood for 17-OHP, cortisol, ACTH, renin, and electrolytes.
key_points: Salt-losing crisis: hypoNa, hyperK, hypoglycaemia, acidosis
Fluid: 0.9 percent saline bolus with dextrose; avoid hypotonic
Hydrocortisone 25 mg IV in infants stat (do not wait)
Draw pre-treatment 17-OHP, cortisol, ACTH, renin
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone at high dose has intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity through renal glucocorticoid receptor spillover; fludrocortisone is added enterally for maintenance once absorption is reliable, not during crisis.

sources.label: Endocrine Society CAH Clinical Practice Guideline 2018

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing epiglottitis from severe croup and initial airway plan
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to resus for a 4 year old boy who was well at breakfast and by mid-morning has become acutely unwell over three hours with a high fever, muffled voice, and refusal to swallow his saliva. He has never had cough or coryza in this illness. He is sitting forward with his mouth open and drool pooling on his chin. He has had all vaccinations except pertussis and Haemophilus influenzae type b which the family declined.

He is not distressed by parents holding him upright but any attempt to lie him supine triggers agitation and worsening stridor.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 38, SpO2 94% in room air, temperature 39.4
data_table.Airway: soft inspiratory stridor at rest, no barking cough, drooling continuously
data_table.General: toxic-appearing, tripoding, refusing all oral intake
data_table.Nil investigations: no lateral neck film, no venous access yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 with oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg and observation for three hours in the resus cubicle
options.rationale: This is the RCH management pathway for severe croup, which presents with barking cough and coryzal prodrome. Rapid onset with drooling, muffled voice and toxicity without cough points to epiglottitis, where instrumentation risks complete obstruction and paediatric anaesthetic-led intubation in theatre is the safe approach. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction

options.text: Perform an urgent portable lateral soft tissue neck radiograph to look for the thumbprint sign before committing to a management pathway
options.rationale: Lateral neck imaging is unnecessary and dangerous - the child must lie back for the film and the film is not diagnostic in a proportion of cases. Bedside clinical assessment plus theatre laryngoscopy is the standard, and imaging causes delay. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction

options.text: Insert an intravenous cannula, take blood cultures, and commence IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg immediately in the cubicle prior to airway assessment
options.rationale: Antibiotic cover with ceftriaxone is appropriate once the airway is definitively secured, but cannulation prior to airway control commonly precipitates crying, complete obstruction and cardiac arrest in suspected epiglottitis. Antibiotics follow the airway, not the other way round. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction

options.text: Keep the child upright with the parent, avoid all examination and cannulation attempts, and call paediatric anaesthetics and ENT for theatre intubation
options.rationale: Toxic child, drooling, muffled voice, absent cough and unvaccinated for Hib fit epiglottitis. Any distress can precipitate complete obstruction, so the safe plan is minimal handling, no throat inspection, keep upright with the parent, and rapid escalation to a senior team who can secure the airway in theatre with a surgical airway back-up. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction

options.text: Trial high-flow humidified oxygen via nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min in the cubicle and reassess in fifteen minutes for improvement
options.rationale: High flow nasal cannula does not treat mechanical supraglottic obstruction and delays theatre transfer. In epiglottitis, oxygen without airway control does not prevent obstruction. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction

explanation.summary: Bacterial epiglottitis is rare since Hib vaccination but resurgent in unvaccinated children. The classic triad is drooling, muffled voice and dysphagia with a rapid febrile onset and no cough. Management priority is airway preservation - minimise handling, no cannulation attempts, no examination of the throat, transfer with the parent to theatre for gaseous induction by an experienced paediatric anaesthetist with ENT stand-by for surgical airway. IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg follows definitive airway control. Household contacts require rifampicin prophylaxis if any contact is under four and unimmunised.
key_points: Drooling, muffled voice, no cough and toxic look = epiglottitis until proven otherwise
Minimal handling; do not lie flat; do not cannulate before theatre
Anaesthetics + ENT in theatre with surgical airway back-up
Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV after airway secure
Rifampicin prophylaxis for unimmunised household contacts under four
explanation.pearls: Consider parainfluenza-mediated bacterial tracheitis in a similar-looking child with cough and thick pus at the trachea on laryngoscopy - IV flucloxacillin plus ceftriaxone is the AU empirical cover.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Acute upper airway obstruction

subtopic_detail: Recognising the conjugated fraction that mandates biliary atresia workup
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the community-linked jaundice clinic reviewing a 3 week old term breastfed girl referred by the child health nurse for persistent yellow skin. Birth weight was 3.4 kg and she has regained above birth weight with normal wet nappies. The mother reports pale putty-coloured stools for the last five days and dark yellow urine that stains the nappy.

Examination shows mild scleral icterus and a soft abdomen with a liver edge felt 2 cm below the costal margin.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Coagulation: INR 1.1 after IM vitamin K at birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother, continue breastfeeding, and review in one week as breast milk jaundice can persist to 12 weeks in well infants
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is entirely unconjugated. A conjugated bilirubin above 25 micromol/L or above 20 percent of total demands urgent workup regardless of how well the infant appears - pale stools plus a raised conjugated fraction is biliary atresia until proven otherwise. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Commence oral ursodeoxycholic acid 20 mg/kg/day and repeat liver function tests in one week to reassess for improvement in cholestasis
options.rationale: Empirical UDCA in an undifferentiated cholestatic neonate delays diagnosis and does not treat biliary atresia. Symptomatic pharmacotherapy is only appropriate once biliary atresia is excluded and a specific diagnosis (e.g. Alagille syndrome, PFIC) is made. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Arrange urgent same-day tertiary paediatric hepatology transfer for structural imaging and biliary atresia workup
options.rationale: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (42 micromol/L is above the 25 micromol/L threshold) with acholic stools in a 22 day old is a paediatric emergency. Kasai portoenterostomy outcomes are best when performed before day 45 to 60 of life, so any hint of biliary atresia mandates same-day transfer for HIDA scan, targeted ultrasound and liver biopsy under a paediatric hepatology team. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Commence single-surface phototherapy at home and repeat total bilirubin in 24 hours per the RCH phototherapy nomogram
options.rationale: Phototherapy addresses unconjugated bilirubin only and does not treat conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Using phototherapy here is inappropriate and dangerously delays biliary atresia workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Send TORCH serology and thyroid function tests and review in outpatient clinic in five days with the results
options.rationale: TORCH and TSH form part of the cholestatic workup but they are done in parallel with tertiary transfer, not instead of it. Waiting five days for outpatient results erodes the window for a successful Kasai procedure. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Prolonged jaundice beyond 14 days in a term infant (21 days if preterm) mandates a split bilirubin. A conjugated fraction above 25 micromol/L or above 20 percent of total defines cholestasis and demands same-day tertiary transfer to exclude biliary atresia. Acholic stools and dark urine are hallmark features. Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy performed before day 45 to 60 of life gives the best chance of a native liver, so time to diagnosis directly determines outcome. Never delay imaging or refer for outpatient follow-up when the split bilirubin is abnormal.
key_points: Conjugated bilirubin >25 micromol/L or >20 percent of total = cholestasis
Pale acholic stools + cholestasis = biliary atresia until proven otherwise
Kasai portoenterostomy outcomes decline sharply after day 60
Same-day tertiary hepatology transfer, not clinic review
Phototherapy has no role in conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
explanation.pearls: Give IM vitamin K 1 mg on transfer to any infant with cholestasis regardless of prior IM dose, because bile-dependent vitamin K absorption is impaired and intracranial haemorrhage risk is real.

subtopic_detail: Discharge planning versus admission after a self-terminating febrile convulsion
stem:
You are the emergency department paediatric registrar reviewing an 18 month old boy brought in by his father after a witnessed generalised seizure at home. The father says his son was hot and grizzly since yesterday, then had a two minute stiffening and jerking episode with no post-ictal focal weakness. Recovery was slow to full alertness over 40 minutes; he is now smiling and reaching for toys.

His older sister has just been diagnosed with adenovirus and he is up to date with vaccinations. He is drinking well from a cup.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 92/56, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 39.2
data_table.Neurological: GCS 15, tone normal, no focal deficit, no bulging fontanelle (closed)
data_table.Cardiorespiratory: clear chest, warm peripheries, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Family history: one paternal cousin had childhood febrile seizures, no epilepsy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit under paediatrics for at least 24 hours of observation, electroencephalography and MRI of the brain before discharge
options.rationale: Simple febrile seizures do not need EEG or MRI. Routine admission is not required if the child has returned to baseline, has a clear infective source and there are no atypical features. Investigations are reserved for complex, prolonged or focal seizures. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile convulsion)

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol and ibuprofen and a written seizure action plan explaining recurrence and simple first aid
options.rationale: A simple febrile convulsion (generalised, under 15 min, one in 24 hours) in a child aged 6 months to 5 years who has returned to baseline can be discharged home with parental education, safety-netting for recurrence, and a plain-language written action plan. Antipyretics do not prevent recurrence but treat discomfort. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile convulsion)

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture and start IV ceftriaxone in the emergency department before any decision about discharge is made
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture is reserved for infants under twelve months, any child with meningism, atypical features, or those on prior antibiotics that could mask meningitis. An 18 month old with normal neurology and clear alternative source does not need LP. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile convulsion)
